r-linear-single.whatItIs: 6-9 people seated in one straight row. Either all face the same direction (usually north) or some face north and some face south, in which case the split is stated as a count and who faces which way must be deduced. Clues use 'kth to the left/right of', 'immediate neighbour', 'n persons sit between', and 'sits at an extreme end'. One diagram answers 5 questions. This is the format that most often carries the alphabetical-rearrangement question in Clerk Prelims.
r-linear-single.coreMethod:
1. Read the preamble and note: how many persons, how many seats (they are equal unless stated), and the facing arrangement.
2. Draw ONE horizontal line with n slots, numbered 1 to n from LEFT to RIGHT. Write W above slot 1 and E above slot n. This is a compass row: for a person facing north, west is on their left.
3. Under each slot leave room for two marks: the name, and a facing arrow (up-arrow for north, down-arrow for south).
4. Direction rule: for a NORTH-facing reference person, kth to the LEFT is -k (toward slot 1) and kth to the RIGHT is +k (toward slot n). For a SOUTH-facing reference person these invert: kth to the LEFT is +k and kth to the RIGHT is -k. As in circular seating, the facing of the person named AFTER 'of' sets the sign.
5. Unlike a circle there is no wraparound. Any computed slot outside 1..n kills that branch immediately — use this, it is the fastest eliminator in the topic.
6. Start with end-anchored clues. 'X sits at an extreme end' gives exactly 2 placements; 'X sits third from the left end' gives exactly 1. A clue with 1 or 2 placements beats a clue with 5.
7. Convert 'n persons sit between X and Y' to |slot difference| = n + 1. In a single row this still gives two placements (X left of Y, or Y left of X) unless the clue says which side, so carry both.
8. Apply positive clues until the row is 60-70 percent full, then sweep the negative clues ('X does not sit at either end', 'X is not adjacent to Y') across the surviving branches in one pass.
9. When 3 or fewer persons remain unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused, brute-force the tail rather than deducing.
10. Verify the completed row against every clue before answering.
11. For the alphabetical-rearrangement question, write the alphabet row underneath and compare column by column — all n columns, no early stopping.

WORKED EXAMPLE (verify it): 7 persons A-G sit in a row, all facing north. (i) C sits third to the right of A. (ii) B sits at an extreme end. (iii) Only two persons sit between B and D. (iv) E sits second to the left of B. (v) F is an immediate neighbour of A.
Clue (iv) with B at slot 1 would put E at slot -1, impossible, so B = 7 and E = 5. Clue (iii): |7 - D| = 3, so D = 4. Clue (i): C = A + 3 with slots 4, 5, 7 taken, so C = 6 and A = 3. Clue (v): A's neighbours are 2 and 4; 4 is D, so F = 2. G takes slot 1.
Final row, west to east: G, F, A, D, E, C, B.
Question: who sits exactly between F and D? Slots 2 and 4, so slot 3 = A. Answer: A.
tricks: ONE ROW, DRAWN ONCE, WITH COMPASS LABELS. Write W and E at the ends before the first clue. In mixed-facing sets this single habit removes the need to think about left and right at all — you only ever think in slot numbers, and the arrow tells you which way to step.

SIGNED SLOT STEPS. Reduce every clue to plus-or-minus a number of slots and write that number in the margin next to the clue. Chained references collapse by addition exactly as in circular seating: for two north-facers, '2nd to the right of the one who is 4th to the left of P' is -4 +2 = -2, i.e. 2nd to the LEFT of P. One glance instead of two hops.

OUT-OF-RANGE KILL. Before drawing anything, scan for a clue that references a fixed distance from a named end. 'E sits second to the left of B' plus 'B sits at an extreme end' collapses to a single placement in one line, because the left end is arithmetically impossible. This one move often decides the whole set in the first 20 seconds.

ALPHABETICAL REARRANGEMENT, DONE CORRECTLY. Write the final row, then write A, B, C, ... in order directly underneath, one letter per slot. A person keeps their position only if their letter sits above the same letter. Check EVERY column — the standard option set is None / One / Two / Three / More than three, and Three is a normal answer. Example: row G F A D C B E with alphabet A B C D E F G underneath gives a match only at slot 4 (D above D), so the answer is One. Never stop the scan early; with 0.25 negative marking a truncated scan converts a free mark into a loss.

GAP ARITHMETIC IN ADVANCE. Before placing anything, convert every 'n persons between' clue to its slot difference (n+1) in the margin. Doing all of them at once takes 10 seconds and prevents the single most common off-by-one in the topic.
traps: For a SOUTH-facing person, their left is toward the EAST end of your drawn row, i.e. toward higher slot numbers. Candidates who drew the row and then reasoned in page-left/page-right terms get every south-anchored clue backwards.
'Third to the left of A' is not 'third from the left end'. The first is relative and needs A placed; the second is absolute. Sets deliberately use both phrasings within the same puzzle.
'Only two persons sit between A and B' means the slot difference is 3, not 2. The margin conversion habit exists specifically to kill this.
'B sits at an extreme end' is TWO placements. Candidates lock onto the left end because that is where the eye starts, then build a row that fails clue four and restart with four minutes gone.

In a mixed-facing set, 'four persons face north' constrains a COUNT, not identities. Assigning north to the first four people you place, because it feels tidy, produces a self-consistent but wrong grid that survives verification against the seating clues while contradicting the facing count.
r-linear-single.timeTarget: At mastery: 7-8 persons, all facing one direction, one variable — 2:45 to 3:30 for the 5-question set including verification. Mixed north/south facing with the split to be deduced — 3:15 to 4:00. Mains, 8 persons plus a second attribute — 4:15 to 5:15. The alphabetical-rearrangement question adds 20-30 seconds on top of whichever band applies and should be budgeted, not squeezed. Anything past 5:00 on a Prelims-level single row in practice is a method fault to review, not a question to push through.
r-linear-single.masteryCheck: Ten consecutive fresh single-row sets under a running clock: 9 or more solved to a unique row, 47 or more of 50 questions correct, average time at or under 3:45, no set over 5:00. Separately, 15 alphabetical-rearrangement questions in a row with 15 correct — including at least two whose key is Three or More than three — each answered in under 30 seconds by full column scan. If you have never keyed Three on this question type, you are stopping your scan early.
questionPatterns: 'How many persons sit to the right of D?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.
'Who sits exactly between F and C?' — five named options plus a 'None of these' style choice.
'If all the persons are made to sit in alphabetical order from left to right, how many will remain in the same position?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.

'Four of the following five form a group based on their seating positions. Which does not belong?' — the shared rule is normally a constant offset or a shared property such as 'both immediate neighbours face south'.
'What is the position of G with respect to E?' — five options such as 'second to the left', 'third to the right'.
'Which of the following statements is TRUE?' — five statements, exactly one of which the final row supports.

r-linear-single.aiPrompt:
You are setting practice material for IBPS Clerk 2026 Prelims Reasoning. Produce ONE single-row seating set to exam standard.

SPEC: 8 persons A-H in a single row. FIVE face north and THREE face south; who faces which way must be DEDUCABLE from the clues, not stated person by person. Use between 10 and 13 clues and print the clue count. At least three clues must constrain facing (for example 'both immediate neighbours of D face south', 'A and the person at the extreme right end face opposite directions'), because facing cannot be pinned by seating clues alone. Include exactly one clue naming an extreme end without saying which end.

VERIFICATION (before showing me anything): solve your own set exhaustively over all 8! seatings crossed with all facing assignments consistent with the 5/3 split, and confirm EXACTLY ONE full solution survives. If several survive, ADD a facing clue and re-solve. If none survives, relax a clue and re-solve. Do NOT assert uniqueness in words — prove it by printing the final row as slots 1-8 west to east with each person's facing, then one line per clue demonstrating that clue is satisfied.

QUESTIONS: 5 questions, each with FIVE options labelled (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) — IBPS Clerk papers have five options, never four. One question MUST be 'if all persons are rearranged alphabetically from left to right, how many retain their position', with options None / One / Two / Three / More than three, and you must show the alphabetical row and the column-by-column comparison in the answer key. Include one 'how many sit between' question and one odd-one-out group question.

OUTPUT ALSO: answer key with one line of reasoning each, and a closing section naming the two clues whose misreading produces the largest wrong grid, with the specific wrong grid each produces.
r-linear-single.blockPlan: Inside a 4-hour day: pair this with circular seating in the same reasoning block, because the sign rule is identical and learning them together halves the total time. WEEK 1: 60 minutes daily — 10 minutes drilling only the direction rule (write ten one-line clues, half with south-facing references, and mark the sign for each; target ten correct in under 90 seconds), then 35 minutes on three untimed sets writing the signed step in the margin of every clue, then 15 minutes verifying clue-by-clue. WEEK 2: 45 minutes — four sets at 3:45 each on a stopwatch, plus 15 minutes on a separate alphabetical-rearrangement drill (ten questions, full column scan each). From mock phase: two sets per day only, but always embedded in a full 20-minute sectionally timed reasoning paper, so you practise the real decision — attempt or skip — rather than the puzzle in isolation.
r-linear-single.weightageNote: Part of the puzzles-and-seating block that carries 15-20 of the 35 Reasoning questions in Clerk Prelims across 3-4 sets, per published 2025 shift analyses. Linear single-row appeared in a majority of 2025 Clerk Prelims shifts, typically with 5-8 persons. Its practical value is higher than the raw count suggests because it is normally the least clue-dense seating set in the paper and because it is the usual carrier of the alphabetical-rearrangement question, which is a near-free mark once the row is built. State it as one of several high-frequency formats, not as the paper's largest single item.

r-linear-double.whatItIs: Two parallel rows of equal size, typically 4+4 or 5+5. One row faces north, the other faces south, and the two rows face each other, so each person in row 1 is directly opposite exactly one person in row 2. Clues mix within-row relations ('second to the left of'), cross-row relations ('X faces Y'), and often a second attribute per person in Mains. This is the hardest routine seating format at Clerk level because every left/right instruction must be signed against the correct row's facing.
r-linear-double.coreMethod:
1. Read the preamble and extract three facts: the size of each row, which row faces north and which faces south, and whether a second attribute exists.
2. Draw ONE grid, not two diagrams: two horizontal lines, columns numbered 1 to n, with W written above column 1 and E above column n. Put the north-facing row on the BOTTOM line and the south-facing row on the TOP line, so both rows are drawn with west on the page-left.
3. Column rule: with both rows drawn west-to-east, the person in column i of the top row faces the person in column i of the bottom row. This is the only pairing you ever use, and it is why you must never reverse one row when drawing.
4. Direction rule for the NORTH-facing row: kth to the LEFT is -k (toward column 1, west) and kth to the RIGHT is +k. For the SOUTH-facing row these invert: kth to the LEFT is +k and kth to the RIGHT is -k. The reference person named after 'of' sets the sign, and their row sets which of the two rules applies.
5. Write the two sign rules on the page, one beside each row line, before you place anybody. You will consult them ten times in the set.
6. Every 'X faces Y' clue is a free column transfer: it costs nothing to apply and it converts a fact known about one row into a fact about the other. Apply all of them the moment either endpoint gets a column.
7. Order the clues by placement count: absolute end clues first, then fixed distances from a placed person, then 'faces' transfers, then 'n persons between' (two placements each), then negatives last.
8. Resolve chained cross-row clues inside-out. 'X faces the person who sits second to the right of Y' means: find Y's column, apply Y's row sign to get a column, then move to the other row in that same column, and that is X.
9. Out-of-range kill: a computed column outside 1..n ends that branch instantly. In a 4-wide double row this eliminates branches faster than any other test.
10. If a second attribute exists, run it as a third and fourth line under the same column numbers and interleave it with the seating — do not fill the seating completely first, because attribute clues routinely kill a seating branch several steps earlier than seating clues would.
11. Brute-force the tail when 3 or fewer persons across BOTH rows remain unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused.
12. Verify the full grid, both rows, against every clue before answering.

WORKED EXAMPLE (verify it): 8 persons. P, Q, R, S sit in row 1 facing SOUTH. W, X, Y, Z sit in row 2 facing NORTH. The rows face each other. (i) Q sits second to the right of P. (ii) R sits at the extreme west end of row 1. (iii) X faces Q. (iv) Y sits second to the right of X. (v) W is an immediate neighbour of Y.
Columns 1-4, west to east. Clue (i): row 1 faces south, so right is -2, giving Q = P - 2, i.e. (P=3, Q=1) or (P=4, Q=2). Clue (ii) needs R in column 1, which kills the first option. So P = 4, Q = 2, R = 1, and S takes column 3. Clue (iii): X = column 2. Clue (iv): row 2 faces north, so right is +2, giving Y = 4. Clue (v): Y's only free neighbour column is 3, so W = 3 and Z = 1.
Final grid — row 1 (south-facing), west to east: R, Q, S, P. Row 2 (north-facing), west to east: Z, X, W, Y.
Question: who faces the person sitting second to the left of W? W is in column 3 of the north-facing row, so left is -2, giving column 1 = Z. Z is faced by row 1 column 1 = R. Answer: R.
tricks: TWO SIGN RULES WRITTEN ON THE PAGE. Before the first clue, write 'north row: L = minus, R = plus' beside the bottom line and 'south row: L = plus, R = minus' beside the top line. Every mis-signed double-row grid traces to reasoning from memory under clock pressure; reading it off the page costs nothing and removes the fault entirely.

'FACES' IS FREE INFORMATION — SPEND IT IMMEDIATELY. The moment either endpoint of a 'faces' clue acquires a column, apply the clue. Candidates commonly park 'faces' clues until the end and then discover they would have collapsed a two-way branch four steps earlier. Applying them on sight typically saves 40-60 seconds on a 5+5 set.

INSIDE-OUT ON CROSS-ROW CHAINS. For 'A faces the one who sits third to the left of B', do exactly three things in order: B's column, apply B's row sign, switch rows in that column. Never try to hold the whole sentence in your head — write the intermediate column number down.

BRUTE-FORCE THE TAIL, WITH A SPECIFIC TRIGGER. Switch out of deduction when 3 or fewer persons remain unplaced across both rows combined AND at least one clue is still unused. Three unplaced gives 6 assignments, testable against two unused clues in about 25 seconds; deducing further at that point normally costs 50-70. Do not brute-force at 4 or more unplaced.

SECOND VARIABLE ON THE SAME COLUMNS. When a second attribute exists, add two more lines under the same column numbers rather than a separate table. Everything then aligns vertically, and a clue like 'the one who likes red faces the one who likes blue' is read off the grid as a column comparison instead of a lookup.
traps: Reversing one row when drawing. If you draw the south-facing row east-to-west because 'they face the other way', column i no longer faces column i and every 'faces' clue becomes wrong. Draw both rows with west on the page-left, always.
Treating the person you face as an 'immediate neighbour'. Neighbours exist only within your own row. Sets exploit this with clues like 'X is an immediate neighbour of the one who faces Y'.

Applying the north-row sign rule to a south-row reference person. The single most common failure in this topic — and because the two rows are symmetric, the resulting grid is often internally consistent and passes a careless check.

'Only one person sits between A and B' where A and B are in different rows. This clue is meaningless across rows and never appears that way; if you find yourself applying a 'between' clue across rows you have mis-assigned someone's row, which is worth 15 seconds to re-check.

Assuming both rows have the same attribute set when the preamble does not say so. In Mains double-row sets with a second variable, the attribute pool is sometimes shared across all 10 persons and sometimes given per row; the preamble states which, and importing the wrong assumption invalidates the attribute half of the grid.
r-linear-double.timeTarget: At mastery: 4+4 persons, one variable — 3:30 to 4:15 for the 5-question set including verification. 5+5 persons, one variable — 4:00 to 5:00. Mains, 5+5 plus a second attribute — 5:00 to 6:30, which at 5 questions is a defensible spend in a 35-minute Mains reasoning section but is usually the wrong first pick in a 20-minute Prelims section. In Prelims treat a double-row set as the last set you attempt, not the first, unless the clue list is unusually short.
r-linear-double.masteryCheck: Ten consecutive fresh double-row sets under a running clock: 9 or more solved to a unique grid, 46 or more of 50 questions correct, average time at or under 4:30 on 4+4 and 5:15 on 5+5. Separately, an isolated sign drill — 20 clues mixing north-row and south-row references, all 20 signed correctly in under 2 minutes, with no reference to written rules. Until that sign drill is clean, do not time full sets; you will only be practising a wrong reflex faster.
questionPatterns: 'Who faces P?' — five options including an 'Other than those given in the options' choice.

'How many persons sit to the right of the one who faces X?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three; note that 'right' here is X's opposite number's own right, which depends on that person's row.

'Four of the following five are alike based on their positions in the arrangement. Which one does not belong?' — the rule is usually 'faces someone at the same column offset' or 'sits at an end of their row'.
'Which of the following pairs sit at the extreme ends of the two rows?' — five paired options.
'If S is related to W and P is related to X in a certain way, then Q is related to whom?' — the relation is a fixed cross-row column offset; find the offset from both given pairs before answering.
'Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding Y?' — five statements, exactly one supported by the grid.

r-circular.whatItIs: A set of 6-10 people placed at equal distances around a circle (occasionally a square/rectangular table, which behaves identically). Each person faces either the centre (inward) or away from the centre (outward). Clues are given as relative positions — 'kth to the left of', 'kth to the right of', 'immediate neighbour of', 'n persons sit between'. You build one seating diagram and answer 5 questions from it. In IBPS Clerk Prelims the circle is usually 8 persons; either everyone faces the centre (easier) or facing is mixed and must itself be deduced (harder). Mains adds a second attribute per person (a city, a fruit, an age) on top of the seating.
r-circular.coreMethod:
1. Read the whole preamble before touching a clue. Note three things: how many persons, whether facing is stated or must be deduced, and whether any clue says 'when counted clockwise/anticlockwise'.
2. Draw the circle ONCE with n tick marks. Label the tick marks 1..n going CLOCKWISE, with 1 at the twelve-o'clock position. Every subsequent step works on these numbers, not on the picture.
3. Fix the person named in the first usable clue at position 1. Rotations of a circle are all the same arrangement, so this costs nothing and saves you ever redrawing.
4. Beside each name write the facing symbol as soon as it is known: a down-arrow for centre-facing, an up-arrow for outward-facing. If facing is unknown, leave the slot blank — never guess it.
5. Translate every clue into a SIGNED CLOCKWISE STEP. Define clockwise as positive.
6. Direction rule (this is the whole topic): the facing of the REFERENCE person — the one named after the word 'of' — decides the sign. For a CENTRE-FACING reference person, kth to the LEFT is +k (clockwise) and kth to the RIGHT is -k (anticlockwise). For an OUTWARD-FACING reference person, kth to the LEFT is -k and kth to the RIGHT is +k.
7. Reduce every position with mod n. Position (1 + k) where the result exceeds n: subtract n. Where it drops to 0 or below: add n.
8. Handle 'n persons sit between X and Y' as TWO cases unless the clue names a direction. Positions differ by (n+1) going one way and by (total - n - 2) going the other; both are legal placements, so open two branches and carry them until a clue kills one.
9. Rank the remaining clues by how few placements each allows and apply the most restrictive first. A clue naming a fixed distance from an already-placed person is more restrictive than one saying 'X is not adjacent to Y'.
10. Negative clues ('X does not sit adjacent to Y', 'X is neither to the immediate left of Y nor of Z') are elimination tools, not placement tools. Apply them only after you have candidate positions to eliminate — using them first wastes 30 seconds.
11. When 3 or fewer persons remain unplaced, switch to brute force (see tricks). Do not keep deducing.
12. Before answering, verify the finished circle against every clue, one line per clue. Thirty seconds here is cheaper than five wrong answers at 0.25 negative each.
13. Answer the questions off the diagram. Re-derive nothing.

WORKED MICRO-EXAMPLE (verify it yourself): 6 persons A-F sit around a circle. A, C, E face the centre; B, D, F face outward. (i) C sits 2nd to the left of A. (ii) E sits 3rd to the right of C. (iii) B sits 2nd to the right of E. (iv) D is an immediate neighbour of A.
Positions 1-6 clockwise. Put A at 1. Clue (i): A faces centre, left = +2, so C = 3. Clue (ii): C faces centre, right = -3, so E = 3-3 = 0 -> +6 = 6. Clue (iii): E faces centre, right = -2, so B = 6-2 = 4. Clue (iv): A's neighbours are 2 and 6; 6 is E, so D = 2, leaving F = 5.
Final clockwise order: A(1), D(2), C(3), B(4), F(5), E(6).
Question: who sits 2nd to the left of F? F faces OUTWARD, so left = -2, giving 5-2 = 3 = C. Answer: C.
tricks: NET-STEP COLLAPSE. Chained references ('the one who sits 2nd to the left of the one who sits 3rd to the right of P') do not need two hops on the diagram. Convert each hop to a signed clockwise step using the facing of that hop's own reference person, then ADD the steps. With everyone facing the centre: 3rd to the right of P is -3; 2nd to the left of that person is +2; net -3 +2 = -1, so the answer is simply the person 1st to the RIGHT of P. Confirm on the diagram in one glance instead of two. Saves 15-20 seconds per chained question, and chained questions appear in most sets. Sign check: this is consistent with step 6 — left is plus, right is minus, for a centre-facing reference.

ANCHOR AT TWELVE O'CLOCK. Always place your first person at position 1 and never rotate the diagram afterwards. Candidates lose 30-60 seconds redrawing when a later clue 'feels' like it belongs elsewhere; it never does, because every rotation is the same arrangement.

BRUTE-FORCE THE TAIL, WITH A SPECIFIC TRIGGER. Switch out of deduction the moment BOTH of these hold: 3 or fewer persons are still unplaced, and at least 1 clue is still unused. Then write the remaining persons in the remaining slots in every order — 2 unplaced gives 2 orders, 3 unplaced gives 6 orders — and test each order against only the unused clues. Six orders against two clues is roughly 20 seconds; continuing to reason clue-by-clue at that stage typically costs 45-60. Do not brute-force with 4 or more unplaced (24 orders is slower than deducing).

ARROW-ON-SIGHT. The instant a clue establishes a facing, draw the arrow. In mixed-facing sets the single most common cause of a fully wrong grid is applying the centre-facing sign rule to an outward-facing reference person; a visible arrow at the reference name makes that impossible.

WRITE 'BETWEEN' COUNTS INSIDE THE CIRCLE. When you resolve a clue like 'two persons sit between P and Q', write the digit 2 on the chord you used. If a later question asks a between-count on the same pair you read it instead of recounting, and if you branch you can see instantly which arc you committed to.
traps: 'A sits third to the left of B' places A, using B as the anchor. Candidates routinely reverse it and place B third to the left of A, which mirrors the entire circle and makes all five answers wrong. The person named AFTER 'of' is the fixed reference.

In mixed-facing sets, the sign is set by the facing of the REFERENCE person, not the person being placed. If B faces outward and the clue is 'A sits second to the left of B', you must step anticlockwise even if A faces the centre.

'Three persons sit between P and Q' with no direction word is satisfied on both arcs and therefore generates TWO cases. Treating it as one placement is the standard way candidates arrive at a grid that fails a later clue and then restart with 6 minutes gone.

'X is neither an immediate neighbour of Y nor of Z' requires eliminating four seats (both sides of Y and both sides of Z). Candidates eliminate Y's two seats, forget Z's, and let a dead branch survive.

A square or rectangular table set where 'persons sit at the corners facing the centre and persons sit at the middle of the sides facing outward' is still a circle of 8 for arithmetic — but the facing pattern alternates in a fixed way stated in the preamble. Candidates import the pattern from a previous set instead of reading this one's.

questionPatterns: 'Who sits second to the left of P?' — with five options, one of which is 'None of these' or 'Other than those given in the options'.
'How many persons sit between Q and T when counted from Q in the clockwise direction?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.

'Four of the following five are alike in a certain way based on their seating and hence form a group. Which one does not belong?' — the rule is almost always a fixed relative offset (each pair is 'immediate right neighbour'), so test the offset, do not guess.
'Which of the following is true regarding S?' — five statements, exactly one consistent with the final grid.

'If all the persons are made to sit in alphabetical order in the clockwise direction starting from A, how many persons retain their original position (excluding A)?' — build the alphabetical circle beneath and compare every position.
'What is the position of R with respect to F?' — five options phrased as 'third to the left', 'second to the right', etc.

r-polygon.whatItIs: Persons seated around a square, rectangle, triangle or hexagon, some at corners and some at the middles of sides, usually with corner-sitters and side-sitters facing OPPOSITE ways. It is a circular puzzle with an extra seat-type layer and extra reading traps.
r-polygon.coreMethod:
1. Convert the polygon into a RING OF DOTS immediately. Draw 8 dots in a circle; mark 4 of them with a small square (corners) and 4 with a dash (mid-sides), alternating: corner, side, corner, side... Start at the top-left corner and go clockwise. Once drawn, the geometry is gone and you solve it exactly as a circular puzzle. This redraw takes 5 seconds and is the biggest single win in this topic.
2. Write the facing rule in the margin as two words, copied from the intro: 'CORNER-IN, SIDE-OUT' (or whatever the paper actually says). Then apply the circular rule per person: facing-centre => left = clockwise; facing-outward => left = anticlockwise. Because corners and sides face opposite ways, ADJACENT seats have opposite left-directions - that is the entire difficulty of polygon sets.
3. Mine the SEAT-TYPE clues first. 'P sits at a corner' restricts P to 4 of 8 dots. Seat-type clues are the strongest clues in polygon sets and must be applied before any gap clue.
4. Use the PARITY SHORTCUT. Number the dots 1..8 clockwise starting at a corner; corners are odd, sides are even. Then: an EVEN gap preserves seat type, an ODD gap flips it. So 'P sits 3rd to the left of Q, and both sit at corners' is IMPOSSIBLE - killed in one second without drawing anything. This is the best polygon trick that exists.
5. Count SEATS, never corners. 'Third to the left of P' counts every occupied seat, corner or side alike.
6. Precompute the opposite distance and write it in the margin: square with 8 => opposite is 4 seats away and is always the SAME seat type (corner opposite corner, side opposite side). Rectangle with 6 (4 corners + 2 mid on the LONGER sides) => opposite is 3 away. Triangle with 6 (3 corners + 3 mid) => opposite is 3 away and a corner is ALWAYS opposite a mid-side.
7. Solve as a circle, then verify by walking clockwise and checking every seat-type clue against corner/side status.
tricks: Redraw as a ring of 8 dots with corners marked. Five seconds, and all the geometry disappears.
Parity: number clockwise from a corner, corners = odd. Even gap keeps the seat type, odd gap flips it. Use this to kill placements arithmetically instead of drawing them.
Seat-type clues before gap clues, always. They halve the board for free.

Memorise the opposite-distance table: square-8 => 4 (same type); rectangle-6 => 3; triangle-6 => 3 (corner opposite mid-side always). Recognising which type sits opposite validates or kills an 'opposite' clue instantly.
A hexagon with 6 persons (all at corners) is literally an ordinary 6-person circle - there is no seat type at all. Do not over-think it; it is one of the fastest sets in a Mains paper.
If the paper puts mid-side persons facing the centre and corner persons facing outward, that is the REVERSE of the common convention. Box it in the margin so you do not autopilot.
In a rectangle with 6, the mid-side seats exist only on the two LONGER sides, so 'sits in the middle of a side' has just 2 valid seats. That is nearly an absolute clue.
traps: Autopiloting the facing convention. The intro states it every time and it is NOT always corners-face-centre.
Counting only corners when a clue says 'third to the left'. Every occupied seat counts.
Assuming a square seats 8. Squares with 4 (corners only) and 12 (4 corners + 8 sides) both appear in Mains.
In a rectangle with 6, assuming 4 mid-side seats exist. There are only 2.

Forgetting that with alternating facings, two adjacent people have opposite left-directions - so 'A sits to the immediate left of B' and 'B sits to the immediate right of A' can point to different seats. Check both.
Treating a hexagon as having corner/side distinctions when all six sit at corners.
Losing 40 seconds redrawing the square accurately instead of converting it to dots.

r-box.whatItIs: A vertical stack of 6-9 labelled boxes, one box per level. Clues fix relative vertical positions — 'immediately above', 'n boxes between', 'above/below'. Mains sets attach a second attribute to each box (a colour, a city, a weight). There is no facing, no left/right and no wraparound, which makes it the most mechanical of the six puzzle formats: it reduces entirely to placing numbers on a one-dimensional line.
r-box.coreMethod:
1. Read the preamble and note exactly one thing before anything else: the numbering direction. Sets say either 'box 1 is at the bottom and box n at the top' or the reverse. Everything downstream depends on it.
2. Draw a vertical strip of n cells. ALWAYS put the physically lowest box at the bottom of your strip regardless of how the set numbers them, and write the set's own numbering in a narrow second column beside the strip. You then reason in physical space, which is intuitive, and answer in the set's language, which is what the options use.
3. Convert every clue to arithmetic on the strip index, counting the bottom cell as 1:
   - 'P is immediately above Q' means P = Q + 1.
   - 'exactly k boxes are between P and Q' means |P - Q| = k + 1.
   - 'P is above Q' means P > Q only — a bound, not a placement.
   - 'only two boxes are above P' means P = n - 2.
4. Rank clues by placement count and apply the most restrictive first. A large gap in a short stack is extremely restrictive: |P - Q| = 4 in a 6-box stack has only two ordered pairs per direction, so four placements total; a bound like 'P is above Q' has many. Always spend the big-gap clues first.
5. Enumerate the placements of your first clue explicitly as a short list, then test each against clue two. Do not carry a vague 'somewhere near the top' in your head — write the candidate index pairs down.
6. Kill branches on out-of-range: any computed index below 1 or above n ends that branch immediately. This is the workhorse eliminator here and it is why box puzzles resolve fast.
7. Defer pure bounds ('above', 'below', 'not at the top') until you have candidate branches to test them against.
8. If there is a second attribute, run it as a parallel column beside the strip and interleave it with the placement work rather than finishing the boxes first.
9. Brute-force the tail when 3 or fewer boxes remain unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused.
10. Verify the finished stack against every clue, then answer from the strip.

WORKED EXAMPLE (verify it): Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U are placed one above another. (i) Only two boxes are between U and Q, and U is above Q. (ii) S is placed immediately below Q. (iii) P is above T and exactly three boxes lie between P and T.
Number positions 1 (bottom) to 6 (top). Clue (i): U = Q + 3, so (Q,U) is (1,4), (2,5) or (3,6). Clue (ii): S = Q - 1, so Q is not 1, leaving (Q=2, S=1, U=5) or (Q=3, S=2, U=6). Clue (iii): P = T + 4, so (T,P) is (1,5) or (2,6). In the first surviving case positions 1 and 2 are already S and Q, so no (T,P) pair fits — dead. In the second case positions 2 and 3 are taken, so (T,P) = (1,5) works, leaving R at 4.
Final stack, bottom to top: T, S, Q, R, P, U.
Check: between Q(3) and U(6) sit R and P — two boxes, correct. S(2) is immediately below Q(3), correct. Between T(1) and P(5) sit S, Q, R — three boxes, correct.
Question: how many boxes are placed between R and U? Positions 4 and 6, so only position 5 — one box. Answer: One.
tricks: BOTTOM-ANCHORED STRIP WITH A TRANSLATION COLUMN. Draw the strip with the physical bottom at the bottom, and write the set's own box numbers beside it. This lets you use physical intuition while still answering questions phrased in the set's numbering. It costs 10 seconds and removes the topic's only real conceptual hazard, which is a top-down numbering scheme.

GAP TABLE FIRST. Before placing anything, convert all 'k boxes between' clues to index differences (k+1) and write the differences in the margin. Doing all of them in one 10-second pass prevents the off-by-one that otherwise costs a full rebuild, and it immediately reveals which clue is most restrictive.

SPEND THE BIGGEST GAP FIRST. In a 6-box stack a gap of 4 has only 2 unordered placements; a gap of 1 has 5. Starting from the largest gap typically cuts the search space by 60-70 percent in a single step and is the difference between a 2:30 solve and a 4:00 solve.

BRUTE-FORCE THE TAIL, WITH A SPECIFIC TRIGGER. Stop deducing when 3 or fewer boxes are unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused: write out the remaining boxes in the remaining cells in all orders (2 unplaced gives 2, 3 gives 6) and test each against the unused clues. Six orders against one or two clues is about 20 seconds. Do not brute-force at 4 or more unplaced.

PARALLEL ATTRIBUTE COLUMN. For Mains sets with a second variable, write the attribute directly beside each cell as it becomes known, never in a separate table. A clue like 'the box immediately above the red box is heavier than S' is then a two-cell vertical read rather than a lookup.
traps: Numbering direction. If the set numbers box 1 at the TOP, then 'above' means a LOWER number, and every gap sign inverts. Candidates who skim the preamble build a perfectly self-consistent upside-down stack and lose all five marks.
'Only three boxes are between P and Q' means the index difference is 4, not 3. This is the single most frequent arithmetic error in the topic.
'P is placed immediately above Q' fixes P = Q + 1. Reversing it to Q = P + 1 inverts the local order and usually still satisfies the next clue, so the error surfaces only three clues later.
'P is above Q' with no distance is a bound, not a placement. Candidates treat it as 'immediately above', commit, and build a stack that fails verification.

In sets that state 'the number of boxes above P equals the number of boxes below Q', the counts are of boxes, not of positions, so with n boxes the relation is (n - P) = (Q - 1). Reading it as position equality gives the wrong equation.
r-box.timeTarget: At mastery: 6-7 boxes, one variable — 2:30 to 3:15 for the 5-question set including verification, so roughly 1:50 to build and 45 seconds to answer. 8-9 boxes, one variable — 3:00 to 3:45. Mains, 8 boxes plus a second attribute — 4:00 to 5:00. In a 20-minute Prelims reasoning section this is normally the first puzzle you should attempt, because a clean box set resolves faster than any other format and the resolution is verifiable.
r-box.masteryCheck: Ten consecutive fresh box sets under a running clock: 10 of 10 solved to a unique stack, 48 or more of 50 questions correct, average time at or under 3:15, no set over 4:15. The accuracy bar here is deliberately higher than for circular or double-row sets — box puzzles have no facing and no wraparound, so an error is an arithmetic slip or a skimmed preamble, both of which are eliminable. Separately: given 10 preambles alone, correctly state the numbering direction of all 10 in under 60 seconds.
questionPatterns: 'How many boxes are placed between R and U?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.
'Which box is placed immediately above S?' — five options including an 'Other than those given in the options' choice.
'Which of the following boxes is placed at the top?' — five named options.

'Four of the following five are alike in a certain way based on their positions. Which one does not belong?' — the shared rule is usually a constant gap from a fixed box, or 'has exactly one box below it'.
'How many boxes are placed above the box which is immediately below T?' — a chained positional question; resolve the inner reference first.
'If box P is related to box U and box S is related to box Q in a certain way, then box T is related to which box?' — establish the constant index offset from both given pairs before answering.

r-floor.whatItIs: A building of 5-9 floors with one person per floor. Clues fix relative vertical positions — 'lives immediately above', 'k floors between', 'lives on an odd-numbered floor'. Mains sets attach one or two further attributes to each person (a car brand, a city, a subject). Structurally this is the same one-dimensional ordering problem as a box puzzle, with 'floor number' replacing 'box position'; the methods transfer without modification, which is why the two should be practised as a pair.
r-floor.coreMethod:
1. Read the preamble and settle the numbering direction first: almost all IBPS sets number the lowest floor as 1 and the topmost as n, but some invert it. Never assume — one line of the preamble decides every clue's sign.
2. Draw a vertical column of n cells with the TOP floor at the top of the page. Write the floor numbers down the side. If the set numbers from the top, write the set's numbers in a second narrow column so you reason physically and answer in the set's language.
3. Convert clues to arithmetic on the floor number, with 1 at the bottom:
   - 'A lives immediately above B' means A = B + 1.
   - 'k floors between A and B' means |A - B| = k + 1. In a one-person-per-floor set, 'k persons live between A and B' gives the same equation.
   - 'only three persons live above A' means A = n - 3.
   - 'A lives above B' is a bound only.
4. Apply the most restrictive clue first, which is normally the largest fixed gap. In a 5-floor building a gap of 3 has only two placements; in a 7-floor building a gap of 5 has only two. Enumerate those placements explicitly as a written list.
5. Kill branches on out-of-range: any computed floor below 1 or above n ends that branch. This is what makes floor puzzles fast.
6. Handle parity clues by counting the actual options, not by feel. With 7 floors, 'odd-numbered floor' means five options (1, 3, 5, 7); with 5 floors it means three (1, 3, 5). Adding 'but not the lowest' removes exactly one.
7. Defer pure bounds and negatives ('does not live on the topmost floor') until you have branches to test.
8. SECOND VARIABLE: interleave it, do not postpone it. After each person placement, sweep the attribute clues to see whether any now kills the branch. Attribute clues frequently eliminate a branch two or three steps before a placement clue would, and postponing them is the main reason two-variable floor sets overrun.
9. Brute-force the tail when 3 or fewer persons remain unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused.
10. Verify the finished building against every clue, then answer from the diagram.

WORKED EXAMPLE (verify it): Five persons A, B, C, D, E live on five floors, the lowest numbered 1 and the topmost numbered 5, one person per floor. (i) A lives on an odd-numbered floor but not on floor 1. (ii) Two floors lie between A and B. (iii) C lives immediately above D.
Clue (i): A is 3 or 5. Clue (ii): |A - B| = 3. If A = 3 then B is 6 or 0, both out of range — dead. So A = 5 and B = 2. Free floors are 1, 3, 4. Clue (iii): C = D + 1, and the only consecutive pair available is (D=3, C=4). E takes floor 1.
Final building, top to bottom: floor 5 = A, floor 4 = C, floor 3 = D, floor 2 = B, floor 1 = E.
Question: how many persons live above B? Floors 3, 4 and 5 — three persons. Answer: Three.
tricks: TOP-OF-PAGE IS TOP-OF-BUILDING, ALWAYS. Draw the highest floor at the top even when the set numbers floors from the top down, and keep the set's numbering in a side column. Every 'above/below' clue then matches the physical direction your eye moves, which removes the topic's only conceptual hazard at a cost of about 10 seconds.

GAP CONVERSION IN ONE PASS. Before placing anyone, convert every 'k floors between' or 'k persons between' clue to |difference| = k + 1 and write the numbers in the margin. Ten seconds for the whole clue list, and it instantly identifies the largest gap, which is where you should start.

LARGEST GAP FIRST, ENUMERATED IN WRITING. In a 7-floor building a gap of 5 has exactly two unordered placements and a gap of 1 has six. Starting at the largest gap and writing the two or three candidate pairs down usually settles half the building in the first 30 seconds. Holding the candidates in your head instead is where rebuild-from-scratch losses come from.

INTERLEAVE THE SECOND VARIABLE. In two-variable sets, after every person you place, run one quick scan of the attribute clues. Attribute clues typically kill a branch two to three steps earlier than placement clues do; interleaving rather than postponing saves 45-75 seconds on a 7-floor two-variable set and is the difference between finishing and abandoning.

BRUTE-FORCE THE TAIL, WITH A SPECIFIC TRIGGER. Stop deducing when 3 or fewer persons are unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused. Write the remaining persons into the remaining floors in every order (3 unplaced gives 6) and test each against the unused clues — about 20 seconds. Do not brute-force at 4 or more unplaced; 24 orders is slower than deducing.
traps: Numbering direction. A set that numbers the topmost floor as 1 inverts every 'above' relation. Skimming this line produces a fully inverted but internally consistent building and costs all five marks.
'Two floors lie between A and B' means |A - B| = 3, not 2. The margin-conversion pass exists to eliminate this.
Parity option counts. With 7 floors, 'odd-numbered' is four floors (1, 3, 5, 7), not three. Candidates who carry the 5-floor instinct into a 7-floor set drop a live branch and reach a contradiction.
'A lives above B' with no distance is a bound, not a placement. Treating it as 'immediately above' produces a building that satisfies the early clues and fails the last one.

In two-variable sets, an attribute clue that names no person ('the one who owns the Honda lives immediately above the one who owns the Kia') is still a placement constraint on the ATTRIBUTE column and must be applied to the grid, not set aside as unusable until the owners are known.

These sit inside the 3-4 minutes per puzzle set that published 2025 Clerk Prelims analyses report for a practised candidate; targets under about 2:30 for a five-question set are not achievable at exam speed once grid-building is counted, and chasing them causes skipped verification and negative marks.

As with box puzzles the accuracy bar is high because there is no facing to go wrong — residual errors are numbering-direction or gap arithmetic, both eliminable. Separately: given 10 preambles alone, state the numbering direction and the count of odd-numbered floors for all 10 in under 90 seconds.
questionPatterns: 'How many persons live between C and E?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.
'Who lives immediately below the one who lives on floor 4?' — five options including 'Other than those given in the options'.
'Which of the following combinations of person and floor is correct?' — five person-floor pairings, exactly one consistent.
'Four of the following five are alike based on their floors. Which does not belong?' — the rule is normally a fixed gap from a named person, or 'lives on an even-numbered floor'.
'How many persons live above the one who owns the Honda?' — a two-variable chained question; resolve the attribute to a floor first.

'If all persons are made to live in alphabetical order from the bottom floor upward, how many will remain on their original floor?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three; compare every floor, do not stop early.

r-floor-flat.whatItIs: A building with n floors where each floor holds two (occasionally three) flats, so the grid is two-dimensional: floors run vertically, flats run horizontally. Typically 8-12 persons across 4-6 floors. Clues combine vertical relations ('immediately above', 'k floors between') with horizontal ones ('same floor as', 'the flat adjacent to'), and Mains sets add an attribute. Some sets leave one or more flats vacant, which changes the counting rules. This is the most structurally demanding puzzle format at Clerk level because a single clue can move in either dimension.
r-floor-flat.coreMethod:
1. Read the preamble twice and extract four facts: the number of floors, the number of flats per floor, whether every flat is occupied or some are vacant, and exactly what the preamble says about how the flats are oriented relative to each other.
2. ORIENTATION IS ONLY WHAT THE PREAMBLE STATES. If the set says 'Flat 1 is to the west of Flat 2', write that at the top of your grid and use it. If the set says nothing about direction, then no question in the set will require a direction, and you must not supply one. Never invent a convention — an assumed orientation produces a mirrored grid that satisfies most clues and fails the questions.
3. Draw a grid: floors as rows with the top floor at the top of the page, flats as columns in the order the preamble states. Label the columns with the set's own flat names.
4. Vertical rule: 'immediately above' means the SAME flat column, one floor up. A person diagonally up-and-across is never 'immediately above'. Write this on the page.
5. Horizontal rule: 'on the same floor as' moves across columns within one row. 'Adjacent flat' means the neighbouring column on the same floor, never the floor above or below.
6. Counting unit: the clue names its own unit. 'Only two floors lie between A and B' counts floors, so |floor(A) - floor(B)| = 3. 'Only two persons live between A and B' counts persons, and in a floor-flat grid this is used when A and B are in the same flat column, counting the persons in that column between them. If a set is genuinely ambiguous about the unit, carry both readings as branches and keep whichever yields a unique grid — do not pick one on instinct.
7. Vacancy changes counting. If some flats are vacant, a person count between two people in the same column is NOT the same as the floor count, because empty flats are skipped in the person count but not in the floor count. Check for vacancy in step 1 precisely so this is decided before you count anything.
8. Order the clues by placement count: clues fixing an absolute floor or an absolute flat first, then vertical fixed distances, then 'same floor' links, then bounds, then negatives.
9. Use out-of-range kills aggressively: any computed floor outside 1..n ends the branch. In a 4-floor building this is very powerful.
10. Interleave any attribute variable with placement, sweeping attribute clues after each person placed.
11. Brute-force the tail when 3 or fewer persons remain unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused: write the remaining persons into the remaining cells in every order (6 orders for 3 persons) and test against the unused clues.
12. Verify the whole grid, cell by cell, against every clue before answering.

WORKED EXAMPLE (verify it): A building has four floors, numbered 1 at the bottom to 4 at the top. Each floor has two flats, Flat 1 and Flat 2. Flat 1 of a floor lies immediately below Flat 1 of the floor above it, and similarly for Flat 2. Eight persons A-H live in these eight flats, one each. (i) C lives in Flat 1 of floor 3. (ii) D lives immediately above C. (iii) E lives on the same floor as D. (iv) A lives in Flat 2 of an odd-numbered floor and nobody lives immediately below A. (v) B lives immediately above A. (vi) F lives in Flat 2 of floor 3. (vii) G lives immediately below H.
From (i), C is floor 3, Flat 1. From (ii), 'immediately above' is the same column one floor up, so D is floor 4, Flat 1. From (iii), E is floor 4, Flat 2. From (iv), the odd floors are 1 and 3; 'nobody lives immediately below A' forces floor 1, so A is floor 1, Flat 2. From (v), B is floor 2, Flat 2. From (vi), F is floor 3, Flat 2. The remaining cells are Flat 1 of floors 1 and 2, and from (vii) G is floor 1, Flat 1 and H is floor 2, Flat 1.
Final grid — floor 4: Flat 1 = D, Flat 2 = E. Floor 3: Flat 1 = C, Flat 2 = F. Floor 2: Flat 1 = H, Flat 2 = B. Floor 1: Flat 1 = G, Flat 2 = A.
Question: who lives in Flat 1 of the floor immediately below the floor on which F lives? F is on floor 3, so the floor below is 2, and Flat 1 of floor 2 is H. Answer: H.
tricks: ORIENTATION LINE AT THE TOP OF THE GRID. Copy the preamble's exact flat-orientation sentence above your grid before the first clue, or write 'no orientation given' if it says nothing. This takes 8 seconds and is the only defence against importing a convention from a previous set — the failure mode that mirrors an entire grid.

COLUMN LOCALITY IN TWO WORDS. Write 'above = same column' and 'same floor = same row' beside the grid. Every clue then routes to exactly one dimension on sight, with no re-reading. On a 5-floor set this saves roughly 30-45 seconds of re-reading across the clue list.

UNIT-TAG EVERY BETWEEN-CLUE. As you read each 'between' clue, write F for floors or P for persons next to it in the margin. In vacancy sets the two give different answers, and tagging on first read prevents a silent miscount that surfaces only at verification.

ABSOLUTE CELLS FIRST. A clue naming both a floor number and a flat ('C lives in Flat 1 of floor 3') places one person with zero branching. Sweeping the clue list once for every clue of that shape, and placing all of them before doing any deduction, typically fills a quarter of the grid in 20 seconds and shrinks everything downstream.

BRUTE-FORCE THE TAIL, WITH A SPECIFIC TRIGGER. Switch out of deduction when 3 or fewer persons remain unplaced and at least 1 clue is unused: 3 unplaced persons in 3 cells is 6 assignments, testable against the unused clues in about 25 seconds, against roughly a minute of continued cell-by-cell deduction. Do not brute-force at 4 or more unplaced.
traps: Assuming a flat orientation the preamble never gave. There is no default in IBPS floor-flat sets — Flat 1 is not conventionally west, north, or anything else, and 'north of' is not a within-floor relation that these sets use. If direction is not stated, no question needs it; if it is stated, copy it verbatim.

Treating a diagonal cell as 'immediately above'. 'X lives immediately above Y' requires the same flat column. Candidates who allow the diagonal produce a grid that passes several clues before failing.
Confusing 'floors between' with 'persons between'. In a fully occupied same-column pair they coincide; in a set with vacant flats they do not, and the clue's own wording is the only authority.

Assuming full occupancy. When a set says 'some of the flats are vacant', the number of persons is less than the number of cells, every count changes, and 'nobody lives immediately below A' no longer forces A to floor 1 — a vacant flat below A also satisfies it. That is exactly why the worked example above states one person per flat.

Applying an 'adjacent' clue vertically. 'The adjacent flat' means the neighbouring column on the same floor. Candidates who read it as 'the flat above' misplace a person and then cannot close the grid.

questionPatterns: 'Who lives in Flat 2 of the floor immediately above the floor on which C lives?' — five options including an 'Other than those given in the options' choice.
'How many persons live between A and D in the same flat column?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.
'Which of the following pairs live on the same floor?' — five paired options, exactly one consistent with the grid.

'Four of the following five are alike based on their positions in the building. Which one does not belong?' — the rule is usually 'lives in Flat 1', or 'lives immediately above someone', or a constant floor gap.
'If E is related to B and C is related to H in a certain way, then D is related to whom?' — the relation is a fixed floor-and-column offset; derive it from both given pairs before answering.
'Which of the following statements regarding F is TRUE?' — five statements, exactly one supported by the finished grid.

r-dmy.whatItIs: Scheduling on a calendar axis - days of a week, months of a year, dates within months, or birth years and ages. Structurally a linear puzzle on a labelled axis that does NOT wrap around.
r-dmy.coreMethod:
1. Write the axis FIRST, in full and in chronological order, before reading any clue. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat Sun; or the specific months named (careful - they are frequently NON-consecutive, e.g. January, March, April, July, and you must order them yourself); or the years listed.
2. For month + date sets (the commonest Mains form), FLATTEN into one line. Four months x two dates = 8 chronological slots. Write them out in order: Jan 12, Jan 25, Mar 12, Mar 25, Jun 12, Jun 25, Sep 12, Sep 25, and number them 1-8. Every 'before/after/between' clue is now an ordinary linear position clue and every gap clue is ordinary arithmetic. This single move is the biggest time-saver in scheduling puzzles.
3. Keep the real dates written beside the slot numbers, because some questions ask 'how many DAYS between' rather than 'how many persons between'. You need both readings available.
4. Translate clues: 'P's exam is three days after Q' => P = Q + 3; 'only two persons have exams between P and Q' => |P - Q| = 3; 'P's exam is in the month having 30 days' => month is in {Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov}; 'P was born in a leap year' => year divisible by 4.
5. Place absolute clues ('P's exam is on Wednesday', 'R goes in the first month'), then the largest gap, then chain by connection.
6. Exploit NO WRAPAROUND aggressively. Sunday has no next day inside the set, so 'P is three days before Q' forces P into Mon-Thu. Write the legal range in the margin immediately instead of testing placements. This prunes far harder than in circular sets and it is the structural advantage of scheduling puzzles.
7. Bring in the second variable (city, subject, gift) after the calendar is fixed.
8. Verify chronologically, first to last.
tricks: Flatten month+date sets into one numbered chronological line of slots. Turns a Mains-'hard' set into an ordinary linear puzzle.
Write the axis before reading the clues. If the months are non-consecutive, ordering them yourself first prevents a whole-set error that is invisible until the questions.

Keep two calendar facts loaded: 31-day months are Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec; 30-day months are Apr, Jun, Sep, Nov. IBPS uses 'the month which has 30 days' as a disguised absolute clue at least once a year.
No wraparound: convert every gap clue into a legal RANGE for the reference person immediately ('three days before' => reference is in the first n-3 slots).
For day sets with two slots per day (morning/evening), flatten exactly as for month+date: 7 days x 2 = 14 slots in one line.

For age and year sets, convert 'A is 6 years older than B' into year arithmetic against the stated reference year and place on the year axis. Then 'what is the age of X' is a subtraction, not a deduction.
Born EARLIER means OLDER. Write that four-word rule at the top of every age set - papers exploit the confusion relentlessly.
traps: Treating the week as circular. Sunday and Monday are NOT adjacent inside these puzzles.
Reading non-consecutive months as consecutive, or writing them in the order the question printed them rather than chronological order.
'Three days after' (gap 3) versus 'three persons between' (gap 4).
In month+date sets, answering 'how many persons have their exam between P and Q' in DAYS instead of SLOTS, or the reverse.
Getting days-in-month wrong (September has 30, not 31) on a clue that depends on it.
Mixing 'older than' with 'born before' in age sets.
Assuming the earliest date in a month+date set is the 1st - the set will specify its own two dates and they are often the 12th and 25th or similar.
r-dmy.timeTarget: 7-day set, single variable: 2:30-3:00. 8-slot month+date with one variable: 3:15-3:45. Month+date with two variables (Mains): 4:00-4:30. That is 30-50 seconds per question.

How many days are there between the birthdays of T and U?
Four of the following five are alike; which does not belong? (usually same month, or same date across months)
Who was born in the year 1994? / What is the age of V as on the given date?
If all persons are arranged chronologically, who comes third?
Who among the following goes in a month having 30 days?

r-category.whatItIs: A puzzle carrying three or more attributes per person - person plus designation plus department plus city, or person plus floor plus car plus colour. Sometimes there is an ordering axis, sometimes it is a pure matching problem with no order at all.
r-category.coreMethod:
1. Count the variables in the intro line and draw a table with exactly that many columns plus the spine column, BEFORE reading clue 1. If you find yourself adding a column mid-solve, you misread the intro - stop and re-read rather than patching.
2. Identify the SPINE: the one variable with a natural order (floor number, seat position, rank, salary, age, date). Put it in column 1, sorted. If NO variable is ordered - a pure matching puzzle such as who plays which sport and lives in which city - do not use a table at all; go to step 6.
3. Tag each clue by how many variables it touches. A clue touching the SPINE plus one other ('the Manager lives on floor 3') is a PLACEMENT clue - use it first. A clue touching two NON-spine variables ('the one who likes red is a Manager') is a LINK clue - hold it; link clues close the puzzle at the end and are useless at the start.
4. Place all spine-absolute clues, then spine-gap clues, exactly as in a floor or box puzzle. Push the spine as far as it will go USING THE SPINE ALONE. Do not touch other columns yet. This spine-first discipline is the entire difference between a 4-minute solve and an 8-minute one.
5. Now attach the second variable using link clues that reference already-placed people, then the third.
6. For pure matching puzzles with no order, use a TICK/CROSS MATRIX: rows = persons, columns = attribute values, cells get a tick or a cross. Rule: one tick in a cell means crosses across the rest of that row and down the rest of that column. After EVERY deduction, sweep for 'only one blank left in a row or column, therefore tick'. That sweep is where most of the deductions come free.
7. Pre-load ALL negative clues ('A does not belong to HR') into the matrix in one pass before touching any positive clue. Each is a free cross and costs 10 seconds total.
8. Hold counting constraints ('there are three females', 'two persons work in Sales') until the end - they are closing clues that force the final two assignments.
9. Verify by reading each completed table row against every clue.
tricks: Draw the complete empty table, all columns, before reading clue 1. Adding a column at minute three means re-writing everything.
Spine first, other variables second, never interleaved.
Pre-load all negative clues in one pass. Ten seconds, and in matrix puzzles they often eliminate a whole branch.
After every deduction, run the 'last blank in a row or column must be a tick' sweep. This is where 3-variable puzzles crack open, and most candidates never do it systematically.
Hold counting constraints for the endgame. Used early they do nothing; used last they close the set.

Abbreviate ruthlessly and write the legend in the margin once (Manager = M, Marketing = Mk). Ambiguous abbreviations produce wrong lookup answers from a correct table - the most annoying way to lose marks.

At the question stage, 'which combination is correct' can usually be answered by scanning the OPTIONS against your table rather than deriving anything - look for the option whose three fields all match a single row.
traps: Mis-counting how many variables exist. Some Mains sets carry four (person, floor, city, fruit, salary) and need four columns.

Assuming 'not necessarily in the same order' applies to every variable when the paper states it for only some. If a variable is listed without that phrase, check whether the printed order is the actual order - rare, but it is a free gift when it happens.

Filling a non-spine column speculatively during branching and forgetting the entries were tentative. In a three-column table you then cannot tell which entries were derived and which were guessed - the set is unrecoverable and you must restart.
Treating a link clue as a placement clue. 'The Doctor lives above the Engineer' tells you nothing until at least one of them is placed.
Answering a lookup question from memory instead of reading the table.
Running past five minutes. A 3-variable set with an ambiguous spine is the commonest time sink in Clerk Mains reasoning.
Choosing the wrong spine - picking the variable with the most clues rather than the one that is ORDERED.

r-uncertain.whatItIs: Puzzles written so that more than one arrangement satisfies every clue, or where clues branch ('either-or', 'at least', 'immediately before or after'). The questions then use 'definitely true' / 'can be true' / 'cannot be determined' language. This is the topic that separates a 40 from a 55 in Mains reasoning.
r-uncertain.coreMethod:
1. DETECT it on the first read. The signature words are: 'either ... or', 'at least', 'at most', 'not more than', 'immediately before or after', 'some', 'may or may not', 'not necessarily'. Also detect it by ABSENCE: if a set of 8 contains no clue fixing a specific seat, floor or day, expect multiple surviving cases.
2. Count the BRANCH FACTOR of every clue before using any of them, and process in ascending order of branch factor - never in printed order. Choosing the right first clue is roughly 80% of your speed on these sets. An 'either P or Q sits at the end' clue branches into 2; an 'at least three persons between' clue branches into 3 or 4.
3. Draw cases side by side, physically separated on the page, labelled Case 1, Case 2, and sub-branches 1a, 1b. HARD RULE: never run more than 3 live branches at once. If a clue would open a 4th, park that clue and use a different one first.
4. Propagate the SAME clue through ALL live cases before moving to the next clue. Solving one case to completion and then starting the next means re-reading every clue twice and is measurably slower.
5. Kill a case the instant a clue contradicts it. Put a large X through it but DO NOT ERASE it - 'which of the following is not possible' questions are answered directly from dead cases.
6. Do not panic when 2 or more cases survive every clue. That is the intended end state, not a failure.
7. Read each question's VERB precisely: 'definitely true' or 'must be true' means true in EVERY surviving case; 'can be true' / 'possibly true' / 'may be true' means true in AT LEAST ONE; 'definitely false' means false in every surviving case.
8. Write the INTERSECTION list once - the facts common to all surviving cases ('A is always at position 2; D is always adjacent to F'). Answer all five questions off that list plus the case grids. This is roughly three times faster than re-reading two grids five times.
9. Trust 'cannot be determined'. If your surviving cases disagree on the asked fact and that option exists, mark it and move on - do not hunt for a clue you think you missed.
tricks: Rank clues by branch factor and use the smallest first. This is the single skill that makes ambiguous sets fast.
Propagate clue-by-clue across all cases, not case-by-case.
Keep dead cases visible with a big X. They are your answer bank for 'which combination is not possible'.
The moment two cases survive, build the intersection list before touching the questions.
The negative half of an either/or clue is free information most candidates drop: 'either A or B sits at the end' also tells you the other one does NOT sit at that end.

Conditional questions ('If P sits at the extreme end, then who sits at position 5?') are free marks when your cases are drawn - the condition simply selects one case. Do these questions first among the five.
Time rule: if a set has 4 or more live cases after 90 seconds, leave it. It will cost six minutes and probably still end ambiguous.
traps: Assuming every puzzle has a unique solution and forcing one, then answering all 5 questions from a grid that was only one of two possibilities. This is the most expensive single mistake in the Mains reasoning section - 7.5 marks gained becomes 7.5 lost plus negative.
Reading 'can be true' as 'is true'.
Erasing dead cases, then having no way to answer the 'not possible' question.
Merging two cases into one diagram by writing alternatives inside the same box.
Treating 'at least two persons between P and Q' as 'exactly two'.
Distrusting the 'cannot be determined' option because it feels like giving up.
Opening a fourth and fifth branch because the clue happened to come next in the printed order.

r-triple-row.whatItIs: Three parallel rows of persons with a stated facing pattern - most commonly Row 1 and Row 2 facing each other and Row 3 behind one of them, or all three facing north. Twelve to fifteen persons. A Mains-level set, and very often the correct set to skip.
r-triple-row.coreMethod:
1. Read the facing sentence TWICE, then draw the three rows in whatever page order makes the facing pairs vertically adjacent. If Row 1 faces south and Row 2 faces north, Row 1 goes on top. A third row facing north behind Row 2 goes at the bottom.
2. Write end-tags on EVERY row - 'L->' or '<-L' per row, using SOUTH = SWAP. Three rows means three chances to mirror, so this is non-negotiable.
3. Number the columns once, from the page-left, above the top row. Column k is the facing-or-behind column across all three rows.
4. Write in the margin exactly which rows face each other and which merely sit behind: e.g. 'R1 <-> R2 face; R3 behind R2'. In a triple-row set usually only ONE pair of rows genuinely faces; the third row carries 'behind / in front of' relations instead.
5. Mine ROW-ASSIGNMENT clues first. Knowing a person's row cuts the board by two-thirds and is worth more than any positional clue. 'P is in row 2' is the strongest clue type in this topic.
6. Solve the row with the most clues completely, then project across columns.
7. Remember that 'how many persons sit to the left of X' is within X's row only.
8. Verify twice: once column by column (facing and behind relations), once row by row (internal gaps).
tricks: Three L-tags before anything else, one per row.
Row-assignment clues before positional clues, without exception.
Write the row sizes at the end of each row. An unequal split (13 persons as 5/4/4) is itself a strong constraint and IBPS uses it deliberately.
If the third row faces nobody, it is an independent linear puzzle joined only by 'behind / in front of' clues - solve it separately and join at the end rather than trying to hold three rows at once.

SCAN THE FIVE QUESTIONS BEFORE SOLVING. If three of them concern one row only, solve that row first and bank 4.5 marks even if you abandon the rest. Triple-row sets reward partial solving more than any other type.
If you have fewer than five minutes left, do not start a triple-row set at all - start the question-scan-and-partial-solve instead and take whatever the first row gives you.
traps: Mirroring one of the three rows. Three rows, three chances.
Assuming all three rows pair up for facing. Only the stated facings exist.
Confusing 'immediately behind' (a column relation between adjacent rows) with 'immediately to the left' (a within-row relation).
Assuming equal row sizes.
Applying a 'faces' clue between two rows that do not face each other. If you think you see one, you have put someone in the wrong row - go back rather than forcing it.
Starting the set with four minutes left and losing all four minutes with nothing banked.
Trying to hold three rows in parallel instead of completing one.

r-inscribed.topicName: Mains puzzles, inscribed circular/square (inner and outer circle)
r-inscribed.whatItIs: Two concentric arrangements - an inner circle or square inside an outer one - typically with the inner persons facing outward and the outer persons facing inward, so each inner person directly faces an outer person. Eight plus eight equals sixteen persons is the standard Mains form.
r-inscribed.coreMethod:
1. Draw two concentric rings with 8 radial SPOKES. Put the dots ON the spokes so that inner dot k and outer dot k are radially aligned. Number the spokes 1-8 clockwise. That radial alignment IS the 'faces' relation - you never compute it again.
2. Write the two direction arrows on the diagram immediately. For the standard 'inner faces outward, outer faces inward' set: the OUTER person faces the centre so their left = CLOCKWISE; the INNER person faces outward so their left = ANTICLOCKWISE. Write 'OUT-L (clockwise)' and 'IN-L (anticlockwise)' on the page. Derive it once from the top-of-circle test rather than trusting memory. If the paper reverses the facing (inner faces centre, outer faces outward - the back-to-back variant), flip both arrows and box the note.
3. THE TWO RINGS HAVE OPPOSITE LEFT-DIRECTIONS. That is the entire difficulty of this topic, and one annotation removes it.
4. Mine all 'faces' clues FIRST. Each one welds an inner person to an outer person on the same spoke and gives you two placements for the price of one. In a 16-person set the facing clues are by a wide margin the highest-value clues.
5. Fix your first placement at spoke 1 (12 o'clock) and never rotate the diagram.
6. Apply gap clues WITHIN a ring only. A clue never counts positions across rings - if it appears to, re-read, because it will be a 'faces' or 'opposite' clue.
7. Use spoke arithmetic instead of counting: '3rd to the left of outer-P' = spoke(P) + 3 (mod 8); '3rd to the left of inner-Q' = spoke(Q) - 3 (mod 8). Opposite within a ring = 4 spokes away.
8. Ping-pong between the rings deliberately: place an outer person, use a facing clue to place the corresponding inner person, then use the inner ring's own gap clues to extend. That alternation is the intended solve path and is far faster than completing one ring first.
9. Verify by walking spokes 1 to 8 and reading each inner/outer pair against every facing clue.
tricks: Two direction arrows on the diagram before you place anyone. The rings have opposite left-directions; this one annotation is worth more than any other trick in the topic.
Facing clues first - each is two placements.
Spoke numbering 1-8 converts every position into an integer, so you do arithmetic mod 8 instead of counting dots and miscounting.

Square-inside-square variants (16 persons, 8 in each square at corners and mid-sides) redraw as two rings of 8 with corners marked; then apply the polygon parity trick (corners = odd spokes, odd gap flips seat type). The two topics collapse into one diagram.

Even a half-solved inscribed set answers the 'who faces X' questions in about five seconds each - that is 1.5 marks per question in Mains for almost no work. Always check the question list for facing questions before abandoning.

'Opposite' and 'faces' are DIFFERENT relations in these sets: 'faces' is radial across the rings, 'opposite' is within a ring at 4 spokes. Write both definitions in the margin so you never conflate them mid-solve.
If the intro says only SOME persons face the centre in each ring, skip - that version does not fit a Clerk Mains time budget unless you have six spare minutes.
traps: Using the same left-direction for both rings. This is the defining error of inscribed sets and it destroys the whole grid, not just one placement.
Assuming inner faces outward. The paper states it and does sometimes reverse it.
Assuming both rings hold the same number of people. 8+8 is standard but 6+6 and unequal counts appear.
Reading 'opposite' as 'faces'. Two completely different relations sharing one diagram.
Counting a gap across rings.
Rotating the diagram to make a clue look right, invalidating everything already placed.
Attempting the set in Prelims. It does not belong in a 20-minute sectional clock.

r-blood-seating.whatItIs: A family seated in a row or circle where positional clues and relationship clues are deliberately interleaved. It is two puzzles fused: a family tree and an arrangement, and the whole method is refusing to fuse them.
r-blood-seating.coreMethod:
1. SPLIT THE PAGE. Left half = family tree. Right half = seating frame. Never draw a relation onto the seating diagram or a position onto the tree. This single discipline converts a 'hard' set into two easy ones and is the difference between four minutes and eight.
2. Build the tree with fixed symbols: + for male, - for female, ? for unknown gender, a double horizontal line for a married couple, a vertical line down to children, and children on one shared horizontal generation line. Generations MUST sit on separate horizontal levels. If you cannot see the levels in your drawing, you have drawn it wrong - redraw before continuing.
3. Resolve GENDER before structure. Gender-carrying words: son, father, brother, husband, uncle, nephew, grandfather (male); daughter, mother, sister, wife, aunt, niece, grandmother (female). Words carrying NO gender: child, spouse, parent, sibling, cousin. Mark unknowns with ? and revisit.
4. Expand chained relations from the INNERMOST noun outward, writing each step down. 'The only daughter-in-law of the grandmother of P' expands as: grandmother of P = G; only daughter-in-law of G = the wife of G's only son. Write G, then the son, then the wife. Never resolve a three-link chain mentally.
5. Use COUNTING constraints as the closer: 'there are only three females in the family', 'there are two married couples'. Hold these until the tree is otherwise complete, then use them to resolve the last ambiguous genders.
6. Now build the seating frame as an ordinary linear or circular puzzle, using ONLY the positional clues that name people directly.
7. Do BRIDGE clues LAST: 'The father of A sits second to the left of A's wife'. Translate first, in writing ('father of A = C', 'A's wife = E'), and only then place ('C sits 2nd left of E'). Those written translations are reusable at the question stage.
8. Verify twice: once against the tree, once against the seating frame.
tricks: Two physically separated diagrams. Non-negotiable, and it is the whole technique.
Translate every bridge clue into names in the margin BEFORE placing. The margin note gets reused when you answer the questions.
Gender-count constraints are endgame tools. Used early they do nothing; used last they break the final tie.

Read the questions before you finish the seating. There is almost always one pure-relation question ('how is P related to Q?') answerable from the TREE alone - bank that 1.5 marks even if the seating never closes.
If the intro says 'three generations', draw exactly three horizontal levels first. The tree then has almost no freedom left and builds itself.

Pre-memorise the standard chains so you never derive them in the hall: 'only daughter-in-law of X' = wife of X's only son; 'brother of the mother' = maternal uncle; 'son of the sister of the father' = male paternal cousin; 'father of the wife' = father-in-law; 'only son of the grandfather' = the father (if the grandfather has one son).
In circular family sets, 'P sits between his son and his wife' is unordered = 2 cases, but the gender information usually kills one of them within seconds - apply gender before branching.
traps: 'Brother-in-law' and 'sister-in-law' are genuinely two-way: spouse's sibling OR sibling's spouse. Branch; never assume.
Inferring gender from a letter (A, B, P, Q) or from a person's position in the family. Never.
Assuming a couple has only the children mentioned unless the word 'only' appears.
Reading 'P is the daughter of Q' as making Q female. It says nothing about Q's gender.
Mixing the tree and the frame in a single diagram - the commonest cause of a seven-minute blood-relation set.
Ignoring the counting constraint ('only two males') and finishing with an unresolved gender that the questions specifically test.
Assuming a cousin's gender. A cousin can be either, and papers exploit this.
Treating 'the father of A' as necessarily seated in the arrangement - in some sets a referenced relative is not one of the seated persons. Check the seated list.
