r-puzzle-marathon.whatItIs: Not a question type - the training protocol that turns individual puzzle techniques into exam score. It builds the two things the 20-minute sectional clock actually measures: set-SELECTION judgement, and grid-building speed under time pressure.
r-puzzle-marathon.coreMethod:
1. BUILD A SET-BANK. Every week collect 30 fresh sets from mixed sources - one Prelims-level PDF, one Mains-level PDF, one daily quiz. Never re-solve a set you have seen: recognition inflates your timings and lies to you about your readiness.
2. RUN THREE SESSION TYPES on rotation:
   TYPE A - ACCURACY (3x/week, 60 min): 8 sets, total-timed but not per-set timed. Goal is 100% correct grids on the FIRST pass. Speed is explicitly not the objective.
   TYPE B - SPEED (2x/week, 45 min): 10 sets with a per-set alarm set to that topic's time target. When the alarm rings you STOP that set dead, mark it incomplete, move on. Score = sets completed correctly within target.
   TYPE C - SELECTION (2x/week, 25 min): put 6 sets on the table with exactly 20 minutes on the clock. Your job is to CHOOSE which 4 to attempt and in what order. Score with negative marking. This is the session that actually raises your Prelims score and it is the one nobody does.
3. THE 30-SECOND TRIAGE DRILL (daily, 5 min): read only the intro line and first two clues of 10 different sets and write GREEN / AMBER / RED plus one reason for each. Then solve two GREENs and one RED and check whether your judgement was right. Within three weeks your triage becomes reliable - and triage is worth more marks than any solving trick.
4. THE ERROR LOG - one line per mistake, four columns: (a) set type, (b) the exact clue you misread or step you skipped, (c) the correct reading, (d) the rule you will apply next time. Review it for 5 minutes before every session. When the same error appears three times, it graduates to a pre-solve checklist item written at the top of your rough sheet.
5. THE ESCALATION LADDER - do not skip rungs. Rung 1: 5-floor and 6-person linear sets. Rung 2: 8-person circular and box. Rung 3: double row and scheduling. Rung 4: polygon and 3-variable. Rung 5: uncertain/multi-case. Rung 6: Mains-only types (triple row, inscribed, floor+flat). Move up only when the current rung produces 9 clean solves out of 10.
6. MEASURE THREE NUMBERS WEEKLY: average seconds per set; FIRST-PASS grid accuracy (percentage of sets where the grid was right without erasing); and triage accuracy (percentage of your GREEN calls that genuinely finished under 3:30). All three must improve together. If speed improves while first-pass accuracy falls, you are practising the wrong thing and must go back to TYPE A sessions.
7. CALENDAR: from now to the October Prelims, spend 60 of your 240 daily minutes on this block. After Prelims, raise it to 75-90 minutes and shift the mix toward Mains types (triple row, inscribed, floor+flat, 3-variable) for the run to 27 December.
tricks: Solve on a single A4 sheet folded into four boxes, one set per box. It forces compact diagrams, which is what the exam's limited rough sheet demands.
Practise reading from a SCREEN and writing only on paper. Reading sets on paper builds a habit the exam does not allow, and it silently inflates your speed by 15-20%.
Time every set with a stopwatch counting UP, not down. Countdowns cause panic-guessing; count-ups build honest calibration.

After every wrong set, do not read the solution - rebuild the grid from scratch and find the FIRST clue where your grid diverged from the correct one. Only that clue matters; everything after it is downstream noise.
Once a week, deliberately solve three sets you would normally skip, with no time limit. This is the only way RED sets slowly become AMBER.
Score every marathon session WITH negative marking applied. Unscored practice quietly teaches you to attempt everything, which is the exact opposite of what the sectional clock rewards.

Keep a one-page 'pre-solve checklist' of your own recurring errors (e.g. 'L-tag first', 'gap = k+1', 'read the note'). Read it for 20 seconds before each session; in the exam, run it mentally before your first puzzle.
traps: Practising only the types you enjoy. Everybody who loves floor puzzles ends up bad at double rows, and the paper does not let you choose.
Re-solving old sets and believing the improved time. Recognition is not skill.
Practising untimed for months, then discovering in the hall that a set you thought took 3 minutes takes you 6.
Solving the arrangement without the five attached questions. The questions are where 'four of five are alike' and 'cannot be determined' skills live, and those are pure marks.
Never practising SKIPPING. If you have never abandoned a set at 90 seconds in practice, you will not do it in the exam - you will sink five minutes into it instead.
Reading solutions instead of re-solving. Reading a solution feels like learning and produces almost none of it.
Chasing 35/35 in practice. The exam rewards 26 accurate attempts over 32 shaky ones, and your practice should reward the same thing.

r-inequality.whatItIs: One or two statements linking single-letter variables with >, <, ≥, ≤ and =, followed by two conclusions labelled I and II, and five options. You decide which conclusions necessarily follow. Prelims uses the symbols directly; Mains often codes them behind arbitrary marks (@, ©, %, $, #) defined in a key shared across the whole set. There is no ambiguity and no judgement involved — the answer is fully determined by the chain, so with a fixed procedure this topic is close to guaranteed marks. The only real skills are normalising the chain in one pass and separating the 'Either' case from the 'Neither' case, which is where almost all lost marks in this topic live.
r-inequality.coreMethod:
1. NORMALISE DIRECTION. Rewrite every statement so all signs point the same way. Convert A < B to B > A, and A ≤ B to B ≥ A. Now every relation reads bigger-on-the-left. Do this in one pass, on paper.
2. LINK INTO ONE LINE on the shared variables, keeping the normalised direction. Example: 'P ≥ Q', 'Q > R', 'R = S', 'S ≤ T' becomes P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T.
3. MARK THE BREAK POINTS. A comparison between two variables is valid only if you can walk from one to the other with every link pointing the same way. A break sits at any variable that is bigger than both its neighbours, or smaller than both. In P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T the walk descends to S and then rises to T, so S is a break: P and T cannot be compared. Circle every break the moment you write the line.
4. '=' IS DIRECTION-NEUTRAL. A flat link belongs to both directions, never creates a break and never weakens anything. Treat the two variables joined by '=' as one variable. So in the line above, T ≥ S = R does give T ≥ R, even though S is the break point.
5. TEST EACH CONCLUSION on three things, in this order. (a) PATH: is there an unbroken same-direction walk between the two variables? If not, the conclusion is false — stop. (b) DIRECTION: does the conclusion's sign agree with the walk? If the line gives P > S, then 'P > S' and 'S < P' are both true, while 'S > P' and 'S ≥ P' are both false. (c) STRENGTH: the derived relation is strict (>) only if at least ONE link on the walk is strict. If every link is ≥ or =, the strongest you may conclude is ≥.
6. REMEMBER > IMPLIES ≥. If the line gives P > Q, then both 'P > Q' and 'P ≥ Q' are true. Check this before marking a conclusion false on sign grounds.
7. MARK EACH CONCLUSION TRUE OR FALSE INDEPENDENTLY FIRST. Only then, and only if BOTH came out false, run the Either-or test.
8. EITHER-OR TEST — all three conditions must hold: (i) both conclusions are individually false; (ii) they are about the SAME two variables; (iii) together they cover every possibility with no gap. Two situations produce this. Case A: the line gives a non-strict relation such as A ≥ D, and the conclusions are 'A > D' and 'A = D' — A ≥ D means exactly one of them holds, so Either is correct. Case B: no relation is derivable at all and the conclusions are exact complements, such as 'A ≥ D' and 'A < D', or 'A > D' and 'A ≤ D'. If the two false conclusions leave a gap — 'A > D' and 'A = D' when NO relation is derivable, since A < D is uncovered — the answer is Neither, not Either.
9. MAP TO THE FIVE OPTIONS. The standard list is (1) Only conclusion I is true, (2) Only conclusion II is true, (3) Either I or II is true, (4) Neither I nor II is true, (5) Both I and II are true. T/F → (1); F/T → (2); T/T → (5); F/F → run step 8, giving (3) or (4).
10. CODED SETS. Write the key vertically in the margin once for the whole set, preserving variable order: 'P @ Q means P is not smaller than Q' → @ means ≥; 'not greater than' → ≤; 'neither greater than nor equal to' → <; 'neither smaller than nor equal to' → >. Translate every statement into symbols first, then run steps 1-9 unchanged.
11. WORKED EXAMPLES. (a) P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T; I. P > S, II. T > R. Walk P ≥ Q > R = S contains the strict link Q > R, so P > S is TRUE. T ≥ S = R gives only T ≥ R, so T > R is FALSE. Answer (1). (b) A ≥ B ≥ C ≥ D; I. A > D, II. A = D. No strict link, so only A ≥ D — both false, same pair, no gap → Either, answer (3). (c) X < Y ≥ Z > W, i.e. Y > X and Y ≥ Z > W; I. X > Z, II. X = Z. Y is bigger than both neighbours, so X and Z are unrelated: both false, same pair, but X < Z is uncovered → Neither, answer (4). (d) L > M ≥ N = O > P; I. L > O, II. M > P. Both walks contain a strict link, so both TRUE, answer (5).
tricks: Normalise everything to one direction on the first pass and commit it to a single written line. Chasing a mixed line such as 'A ≤ B > C ≥ D' while you evaluate each conclusion is where re-reads happen; a single-direction line turns every conclusion into a left-to-right glance. That is 5-8 seconds saved per conclusion, and a five-question set has ten conclusions.
Underline the strict links (> only) as you write the normalised line. Step 5c then reduces to 'is there an underline anywhere between these two letters?', with no re-scan of the chain.
Circle the break points immediately after writing the line. Every no-relation conclusion, every Neither and every Case-B Either in the set then falls out of those circles without further reasoning.
Because > implies ≥, a line giving P > Q makes both 'P > Q' and 'P ≥ Q' true. Checking the conclusion's sign against the derived one recovers marks that are otherwise dropped as 'wrong symbol'.

Run the Either-or test only on F/F pairs, and check its three conditions in the order same-pair first, gap second. Most F/F pairs fail the same-pair condition in under two seconds, so you never spend time reasoning about exhaustiveness on a pair that could never qualify.

In coded sets the key is shared by all four or five questions. Translate it once into a five-line symbol table in the margin; re-reading the wordy key per question costs roughly ten seconds five times over.
traps: Concluding a strict > from a walk made entirely of ≥ and =. 'A ≥ B ≥ C' does not give 'A > C'. This is the single largest source of wrongly-marked 'Both are true' answers in this topic.

Marking Neither for every F/F pair. An F/F pair on the same two variables with no gap in coverage is Either — a different option, and the five choices contain both precisely to separate the two cases.

Marking Either whenever both conclusions are false and share their variables, without checking for a gap. 'A > C' and 'A = C' with no derivable relation leaves A < C uncovered, so the answer is Neither.

Reading the conclusion's variables in the chain's order instead of the conclusion's own order. If the line gives P > S, then 'S > P' is false while 'S < P' is true — the same fact written two ways, and the option list carries distractors for both readings.
Treating '=' as a break in the chain. It is not: P > Q = R gives P > R at full strength, and R = S ≤ T still gives T ≥ R.

Reversing the variable order when decoding. 'P @ Q means P is not greater than Q' is ≤, not ≥, and 'neither greater than nor equal to' is <, not ≤. Write the phrase out as a bare symbol before you use it anywhere.

Assuming that two letters printed on the same normalised line must be comparable. The printed line is not automatically a chain — only an unbroken same-direction walk between them makes a comparison valid.

A coded set: about 15 seconds once for the key, then 20-25 seconds per question, so five questions in roughly 2 min 15 s. r-inequality.masteryCheck: You score 20/20 on twenty fresh direct-inequality questions in under six minutes, and specifically: every Either item is correctly separated from every Neither item when tested on pairs whose conclusions are worded identically but which differ in whether a relation is derivable; you never conclude a strict > from an all-≥ walk; and you can state the break point of a mixed chain such as 'A ≤ B > C = D ≥ E' — it is B — within ten seconds of first reading it.
questionPatterns: Statements: P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T. Conclusions: I. P > S. II. T > R. Options: (1) Only conclusion I is true (2) Only conclusion II is true (3) Either I or II is true (4) Neither I nor II is true (5) Both I and II are true. Answer (1): the walk P ≥ Q > R = S carries the strict link Q > R, so I is true; T ≥ S = R yields only T ≥ R, so II is false.

Statements: A ≥ B ≥ C ≥ D. Conclusions: I. A > D. II. A = D. Same five options. Answer (3): no link is strict, so only A ≥ D follows; both conclusions are individually false, they concern the same pair, and A > D or A = D covers A ≥ D with no gap.

Statements: X < Y ≥ Z > W. Conclusions: I. X > Z. II. X = Z. Same five options. Answer (4): normalised, Y > X and Y ≥ Z > W, so Y is bigger than both neighbours and X and Z are unrelated; both conclusions are false, and their union misses X < Z, so there is a gap and the answer is Neither rather than Either.
Statements: L > M ≥ N = O > P. Conclusions: I. L > O. II. M > P. Same five options. Answer (5): L > M is a strict link on the walk to O, and O > P is a strict link on the walk from M, so both hold.

Coded. Key: 'D % E' means D is greater than E; 'E © F' means E is not smaller than F; 'F # G' means F is smaller than G. Statements: D % E, E © F, F # G. Conclusions: I. D > G. II. G ≥ E. Same five options. Answer (4): the line is D > E ≥ F and G > F, so F is smaller than both its neighbours and both conclusions cross that break and are false; they also concern different variable pairs, (D,G) and (G,E), so Either cannot apply.

r-coded-ineq.whatItIs: Symbols (@, #, $, %, &) are defined as inequality relations, usually in deliberately awkward negative language. You decode, then solve exactly as direct inequality. In Mains this also appears as the 'resultant' variant where you pick the symbol that makes a stated relation true.
r-coded-ineq.coreMethod:
1. Before touching any question, build a DECODE BOX at the top of the rough sheet: five lines, symbol on the left, single sign on the right. This costs 30-40 seconds once and serves the entire 5-question set.
2. Translate the negative wording mechanically. Memorise these five conversions — they cover essentially every definition IBPS writes:
   • 'not greater than' = ≤
   • 'not smaller/less than' = ≥
   • 'neither greater than nor equal to' = <
   • 'neither smaller than nor equal to' = >
   • 'neither greater than nor smaller than' = =
   The logic: NOT of a strict sign gives the opposite sign WITH equality attached. 'Neither X nor Y' leaves the one remaining primitive out of {>, <, =}.
3. Check letter order in the definition. 'P @ Q means P is not smaller than Q' defines P relative to Q. If the question writes 'Q @ P', the relation is Q ≥ P, not P ≥ Q.
4. Write the decoded sign in pencil directly ABOVE each symbol in the question expression. Now the line reads as a normal inequality.
5. DECODE THE CONCLUSIONS TOO. They are written in the same symbol language. Half of all errors in this topic come from decoding the statement and then comparing against an un-decoded conclusion.
6. Solve using the direct-inequality method: trace the segment, find the flip, apply the weakest-link rule, run the either-or test.
7. Resultant/symbol-substitution variant: you are given an expression with a blank and a target relation. Take each option, slot its symbols in, and test only the segment between the two target variables. Do not evaluate the whole chain.
tricks: One decode box per set, drawn before you read a single question. Every subsequent question becomes a 25-second direct-inequality problem. Re-reading the definition block five times is how aspirants lose 90 seconds on a 5-question set.
Convert the definition text into a single character immediately — write '@ = ≥' not '@ means not smaller than'. Never leave prose on your rough sheet; prose has to be re-parsed.
'Neither A nor B' → there are only three primitives {>, <, =}; strike the two named and take the survivor. Two seconds, no thinking.
Write the decoded sign ABOVE the symbol inside the printed question rather than transcribing the whole expression. Saves 10-15 seconds per question and eliminates copy errors.
In symbol-substitution questions, check each option's FIRST symbol against the required direction first — a wrong-direction first symbol usually kills the option without reading the rest.
Re-read the definition block when a new set begins. IBPS routinely reuses @ and # with different meanings in a second set on the same paper.
traps: Decoding 'not greater than' as < instead of ≤. Costs one to two marks in nearly every paper that carries this topic.
Decoding the statement but forgetting the conclusions are also coded.
Reversing the letter order: the definition says 'P @ Q means P is not smaller than Q', and the question uses 'Q @ P' — the relation flips.
Carrying a decode box forward from an earlier set on the same paper.
Skipping the either-or check because the decoding already ate your time budget — the either-or questions are still there and are still worth a full mark.
Assuming every set defines exactly five symbols. Some define four, some six; count them into the box.
In resultant-type questions, evaluating the whole expression when only the segment between the two target letters matters.

r-syllogism.whatItIs: Two or three statements using All / Some / No / Only / Only a few, followed by two conclusions (sometimes including possibility conclusions). You decide what definitely follows. Rule-driven, and faster without Venn diagrams once the table is memorised.
r-syllogism.coreMethod:
1. Convert each statement to shorthand BEFORE reading the conclusions:
   • All A are B → A sits fully inside B
   • Some A are B → A and B overlap
   • No A is B → A and B are disjoint
   • 'Only A are B' → ALL B ARE A. This is a reversal. Write the reversed form on your sheet immediately; reading it forward destroys the question.
   • 'Only a few A are B' → gives you TWO definite facts: Some A are B (true) AND Some A are not B (true). Modern bank keys treat plain 'Few A are B' the same way.
2. Apply the combination table. Memorise it; do not re-derive:
   • All + All → All (A⊂B, B⊂C ⟹ All A are C)
   • All + No → No (A⊂B, B∩C=∅ ⟹ No A is C)
   • Some + All → Some (Some A are B, B⊂C ⟹ Some A are C)
   • Some + No → Some not (Some A are B, No B is C ⟹ Some A are not C)
   • No + All (reversed middle) → No (No A is B, All C are B ⟹ No A is C)
   • All + Some → NOTHING
   • Some + Some → NOTHING
   • No + No → NOTHING
3. Free immediate conversions — these answer many conclusions with no work:
   • All A are B ⟹ Some B are A ⟹ Some A are B
   • No A is B ⟹ No B is A ⟹ Some A are not B
   • Some A are B ⟹ Some B are A
   • Some A are NOT B ⟹ NOTHING reversible. 'Some B are not A' does not follow.
4. POSSIBILITY conclusions ('Some A are C is a possibility'): your default answer is FOLLOWS. A possibility fails only when the statements make it strictly impossible — which requires an 'All' or 'No' barrier forcing the two sets apart or one inside another. Scan for that barrier; if there is none, mark it true.
5. EITHER-OR: when both conclusions are individually false, share the same subject-predicate pair, and are complementary, mark either-or. The only two complementary shapes are {Some A are B / No A is B} and {All A are B / Some A are not B}.
6. Draw a Venn only when three statements chain through two middle terms and the table result is unclear. Draw the most restrictive diagram first; if the conclusion survives that, test one alternative diagram.
tricks: 'Only a few X are Y' gives you a free 'Some X are not Y'. Aspirants who read it as plain 'Some' throw away a definite fact that is often exactly what a conclusion asks for. Write both facts down the moment you see the phrase.
'Only X are Y' means 'All Y are X'. Write the reversal on the rough sheet in the correct direction before doing anything else — reading it forward is an instant zero on the whole question.
Do possibility conclusions FIRST. They take about 5 seconds each (default TRUE unless a No/All barrier exists) and they are usually the second conclusion in the pair.
Refuse to draw Venn diagrams for two-statement questions. The table is 3x faster and just as reliable. Reserve drawing for three-statement chains only.
'Some ... are not' is a one-way street. The instant you see it in a conclusion, check whether it was derived by reversing another 'some are not' — if so, it is false.
When both conclusions are false, spend 5 seconds testing the two complementary shapes before writing 'neither follows'.
If a conclusion links two terms that share no middle term across the statements, mark it false without analysis.
traps: Reversing 'Some A are not B' into 'Some B are not A'. Never valid, and IBPS tests it constantly.
Treating 'Only a few' as merely 'Some' and losing the free 'Some are not'.
Reading 'Only A are B' forward as 'All A are B' instead of 'All B are A'.
Marking a possibility conclusion FALSE because it is not proven. Possibility only requires that it is not forbidden.
Assuming 'All A are B' yields 'All B are A'. It yields only 'Some B are A'.
Missing either-or when both conclusions are individually false — this is keyed in roughly one question per set.
In three-statement sets, chaining two terms that have no common middle term.
Spending 3 minutes drawing every possible Venn arrangement. Two diagrams is the maximum any Clerk-level syllogism needs.
r-syllogism.timeTarget: 25-35 seconds per question once the table is automatic. A 3-question set in about 90 seconds. Three-statement Mains sets: up to 45 seconds per question.
r-syllogism.masteryCheck: You answer 15 syllogism questions — including at least 3 using 'Only a few', 2 using 'Only', and 2 possibility conclusions — in under 8 minutes with 14/15 correct, while drawing no more than two Venn diagrams in the entire set.

r-syllogism-rev.whatItIs: Reverse syllogism gives you the CONCLUSIONS and four or five candidate statement-sets; you pick the set that makes those conclusions follow. Mixed syllogism combines definite and possibility conclusions with 'Only a few' statements. Both are Mains-level and are the reason many aspirants abandon syllogism blocks.
r-syllogism-rev.coreMethod:
1. Reverse syllogism — never solve all options forward. Use three elimination filters in this order:
   • FILTER 1 (connection): does the option connect the two terms in the conclusion through a shared middle term? If a term in the conclusion appears in only one statement of the option, or the two statements share no common term, kill it. Typically removes two options in about 20 seconds.
   • FILTER 2 (strength): match the conclusion's strength to what its parent combination can produce.
     — A definite 'All A are C' can ONLY come from All + All. Any option whose linking statement is 'Some' or 'Only a few' is dead.
     — A definite 'No A is C' can only come from All + No, or No + All (with the All pointing into the No's term).
     — 'Some A are not C' can come from Some + No, from No + All, or from an 'Only a few' statement directly.
     — 'Some A are C' can come from All + All, Some + All, or 'Only a few'.
   • FILTER 3 (direction): check the subject-predicate order in the surviving option's statements. 'All B are C' and 'All C are B' behave completely differently.
2. Only after all three filters, verify the one or two survivors forward using the standard combination table.
3. Mixed syllogism — split the conclusions before working:
   • Answer every POSSIBILITY conclusion first. Default TRUE unless a definite 'No' or a total-containment 'All' forbids it. About 5 seconds each.
   • Answer definite conclusions using the standard table.
   • There is never an either-or relationship between a possibility conclusion and a definite conclusion — evaluate them independently.
4. 'Which conclusion is definitely FALSE' variant: look for the conclusion that contradicts a definite No or a definite All. Only definite statements can make something definitely false.
5. 'Which additional statement would make conclusion I follow' variant: identify the missing link. If the conclusion is 'All A are C' and you already have 'All A are B', the required statement is 'All B are C' — construct it, then match to an option.
tricks: Run the connection filter before reading any option in detail. Two of five options usually fail it outright, which turns a 5-option problem into a 3-option problem in 20 seconds.

Memorise the one-line strength rule: 'ALL comes only from ALL + ALL'. Any reverse-syllogism option offering a 'Some' as its link cannot produce a definite All conclusion. This single rule resolves a large share of reverse questions.
In mixed sets, sweep the possibility conclusions first and bank those marks before the definite ones eat your clock.
When the conclusion is 'Some A are not C', scan the options for the word 'No' or the phrase 'Only a few'. Those are the only two producers.
If two surviving options differ only in the direction of one statement ('All B are C' vs 'All C are B'), you do not need to solve both — the conclusion's direction tells you which one is required.
Do not draw Venn diagrams during elimination. Draw only to verify the single surviving option.
traps: Solving all four or five options forward. This is a 3-minute mistake on a 1.5-mark question.
Accepting an option whose link statement is 'Some' for a definite 'All' conclusion.
Treating 'Only a few A are B' in a reverse option as though it were 'All'. It is Some + Some-not.
Reading an option's statements in the printed order and assuming the middle term sits where you expect — always check subject and predicate explicitly.
In mixed sets, over-analysing possibility conclusions. One consistent arrangement is enough; you are not required to prove it holds in all arrangements.
Assuming that if a definite conclusion fails, its possibility version also fails. The opposite is usually true — the possibility version normally follows.
Applying either-or logic between a possibility conclusion and a definite conclusion.

On mixed sets, you answer every possibility conclusion in under 10 seconds each.

r-series-alpha.whatItIs: A single printed line of roughly 26-30 elements mixing capital letters, single digits and symbols (%, @, #, $, *, &, ©). The line is given once and 3-5 questions hang off it. Only two question families exist: (a) neighbour-condition counting — 'how many digits are immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by a letter?'; (b) positional arithmetic — 'which element is 3rd to the left of the 8th from the left end?', 'how many elements lie between the 7th from the left and the 5th from the right?'. Nothing has to be known or memorised. The whole topic is a disciplined single scan plus two pieces of arithmetic, which is why it is worth building into a reflex before the 20-minute sectional clock ever starts.
r-series-alpha.coreMethod:
1. SETUP, ONCE PER SET. As you read the line the first time, put a light tick above the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th and 25th elements. This is the only setup cost and it serves every question in the set.
2. Count the total number of elements, n, and write it in the margin. Every 'from the right' conversion needs it. Use the worked line below: 7 P % 3 K @ 9 F # 2 M B 5 $ 8 R * 4 W 6 & N 1 T © J — here n = 26.
3. Identify the three families: letters, digits, symbols. For each question note which family the TARGET belongs to and which family each NEIGHBOUR must belong to.
4. NEIGHBOUR COUNTING. Rewrite the condition as a fixed left-to-right window before you scan. 'Digits immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by a letter' becomes the 3-slot template [S][D][L]. Write 'S D L' in the margin.
5. Sweep the line ONCE, left to right, sliding that window. Stop only where the MIDDLE slot matches (here, only at digits); only then look at the two neighbours. Do not run one sweep per condition.
6. Tally with tick-marks on paper, not in your head, then count the ticks. On the worked line the qualifying digits are 3 (pos 4), 9 (pos 7), 2 (pos 10), 8 (pos 15), 4 (pos 18) — five.
7. POSITIONAL ARITHMETIC. Every such question has an ANCHOR (the '...th from the left/right' part) and a SHIFT (the '...th to the left/right of' part). Two rules, and the answer is always counted from the ANCHOR's end:
   - SAME word on both sides (left...left, or right...right) → SUBTRACT: answer position = anchor − shift.
   - DIFFERENT words (left...right, or right...left) → ADD: answer position = anchor + shift.
   Mnemonic: Same → Subtract, both begin with S.
8. WORKED, all four cases, on the line above:
   - '3rd to the LEFT of the 8th from the LEFT' — same word → 8 − 3 = 5th from the left → K.
   - '4th to the RIGHT of the 6th from the LEFT' — different words → 6 + 4 = 10th from the left → 2.
   - '5th to the LEFT of the 7th from the RIGHT' — different words → 7 + 5 = 12th from the right.
   - '3rd to the RIGHT of the 9th from the RIGHT' — same word → 9 − 3 = 6th from the right → &.
9. CONVERT ENDS ONLY AT THE END: kth from the right = (n + 1 − k)th from the left. With n = 26, the 12th from the right = 27 − 12 = 15th from the left → 8.
10. 'HOW MANY ELEMENTS BETWEEN'. Convert both markers to left-positions, subtract, then subtract 1 more. Between the 7th from the left (position 7) and the 5th from the right (position 27 − 5 = 22): 22 − 7 − 1 = 14 elements.
11. Read the element off using your blocks-of-five ticks and match it to one of the five printed options. If your computed position lands above n or below 1, you added where you should have subtracted — go back to step 7 rather than recounting the line.
tricks: Tick positions 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 during the first read. Afterwards every lookup is 'nearest tick, then step 1-2 across' instead of counting from element 1. That is roughly 8-10 seconds saved on each positional question, and a set normally contains two or three of them.

Anchor the scan on the middle slot of the window, not on the neighbours. Only about a third of the line is digits, so a [S][D][L] template makes you test neighbours about nine times instead of inspecting all 26 positions — close to half the scanning time of the naive method.

'Symbols immediately followed by a digit' and 'digits immediately preceded by a symbol' describe the identical adjacent pair, so their counts are always equal. On the worked line both are five. If two questions in a set reduce to the same pair, count once and answer both — but compare the FULL templates first, because an extra condition on either side breaks the equivalence.

Write the end-letter next to every computed number before converting: '12 R', then '= 15 L' using n + 1 = 27. Doing the subtraction in writing rather than in your head removes the single most common cause of a re-count.
For 'immediately preceded by' the target can never be position 1, and for 'immediately followed by' it can never be position n. Skip both ends by reflex instead of testing them.
traps: 'X immediately preceded by Y' means Y sits to the LEFT of X in print; 'X immediately followed by Y' means Y sits to the RIGHT. Flipping these produces an answer that is itself one of the five options, so the mistake never announces itself.

Losing the word 'immediately'. Without it, 'a digit preceded by a symbol' means a symbol anywhere further left, which gives a far larger count. Check for the word before scanning; exam wording almost always includes it, and its absence changes the whole question.
Counting the anchor element as the first step of the shift. '3rd to the left of the 8th' means move three whole places from position 8, landing on 5 — not on 6.

Using the wrong n. n is the count of every printed element including symbols, not the count of letters or the count of one family. Also, if a question restricts attention to part of the line, the (n + 1 − k) conversion no longer applies to that sub-range.
Treating '©', '&' or '$' as anything other than one element each, or treating the printed gaps as elements. Only the characters count.
Assuming the line follows alphabetical or numerical order and answering from the alphabet instead of from print position. F sitting at position 8 has nothing to do with F being the sixth letter.

A full 5-question Mains set: 2 min 15 s to 2 min 45 s including setup. A standalone Prelims question with no set attached: 30-35 seconds including reading the line.

questionPatterns: Arrangement: 7 P % 3 K @ 9 F # 2 M B 5 $ 8 R * 4 W 6 & N 1 T © J. How many digits are there in the above arrangement, each of which is immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by a letter? (1) Two (2) Three (3) Four (4) Five (5) More than five — Answer (4): the digits 3, 9, 2, 8 and 4, at positions 4, 7, 10, 15 and 18.
Same arrangement. Which element is 3rd to the left of the 8th element from the left end? (1) K (2) @ (3) 3 (4) 9 (5) % — Answer (1): same word both sides, so 8 − 3 = 5th from the left, which is K.

Same arrangement. Which element is 5th to the left of the 7th element from the right end? (1) R (2) $ (3) 8 (4) 5 (5) * — Answer (3): words differ, so 7 + 5 = 12th from the right; with n = 26 that is the 27 − 12 = 15th from the left, which is 8.

Same arrangement. How many letters are there in the above arrangement, each of which is immediately preceded by a digit? (1) Five (2) Six (3) Seven (4) Eight (5) None of these — Answer (3): P, K, F, M, R, W and T.

Same arrangement. How many elements lie between the 7th element from the left end and the 5th element from the right end? (1) Twelve (2) Thirteen (3) Fourteen (4) Fifteen (5) Sixteen — Answer (3): positions 7 and 22, so 22 − 7 − 1 = 14.

Each set is one line of EXACTLY 26 elements mixing capital letters, single digits and symbols (use only % @ # $ * & © + = ?), single-spaced, with no element repeated more than twice. Under each line give 5 questions, each with EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (1) to (5) — IBPS Clerk papers always have five options, never four. Question mix per set: two positional questions (one of the form 'Xth to the left of the Yth from the left end', one of the form 'Xth to the left or right of the Yth from the right end'), two neighbour-condition counting questions (one single-condition, one two-condition using both 'immediately preceded by' and 'immediately followed by'), and one 'how many elements lie between' question. Word numeric-count options as Two / Three / Four / Five / More than five, or use None of these as option (5). After all three sets, print a separate answer key that shows, for each question, the computed position or the full list of qualifying elements, so I can check my working. Before printing any question, verify its answer against your own arrangement and confirm the answer actually appears among its five options; discard and regenerate any question that fails this check.
r-series-alpha.blockPlan: Four 45-minute blocks, then maintenance. Block 1: write a one-card rule sheet (Same word → Subtract; Different words → Add; answer always counted from the anchor's end; kth from right = (n+1−k)th from left) and drill 20 positional questions only, no counting questions, targeting 15 seconds each. Block 2: 15 single-condition counting questions using the one-sweep window method, timing each individually. Block 3: 10 two-condition questions plus 10 'how many between' conversions, until the (n+1−k) step is automatic. Block 4: five complete mixed sets under a 2 min 45 s clock each, then re-attempt only the questions you missed. Maintenance thereafter: one 5-question set as a 3-minute warm-up at the start of every reasoning session.
r-series-alpha.weightageNote: Roughly 4-5 questions in Prelims reasoning (out of 35) and 3-4 in Mains reasoning (out of 40), usually as one 5-question set plus the occasional standalone item. It carries a high marks-per-minute rate because it needs no rule-learning, only a disciplined scan — but it is one of several such fast-scoring reasoning topics, not the largest single contributor to the section.

r-series-num.whatItIs: Two related question types. In a NUMBER SERIES you are given five or six terms and must supply the missing term, or identify the one term that breaks the pattern (the 'wrong number' variant). In a LETTER or ALPHANUMERIC SERIES you are given letters, or a mixed string of letters, digits and symbols, and must supply the next element or answer positional questions about the string. Both are single-question items: no shared diagram, no set. That makes them the fastest-scoring and fastest-abandoning items in the Reasoning paper — the discipline of quitting on time matters as much as the method.
r-series-num.coreMethod:
1. Decide the variant in the first three seconds: missing term, wrong term, or alphanumeric string. The three have different procedures and mixing them wastes the whole time budget.
2. NUMBER SERIES, PASS ONE — first differences. Write the differences between consecutive terms in a row underneath. If the differences are constant, or form an obvious sequence (arithmetic, squares, cubes, primes, factorials), you are done. If not, write the second differences. Stop after second differences; a third row almost never resolves at Clerk level.
3. NUMBER SERIES, PASS TWO — ratios and hybrids. Divide each term by the previous one. If the ratios are near-integer and drifting upward, test the hybrid family: multiply by n and add or subtract k, with n incrementing (times 1 plus 1, times 2 plus 2, times 3 plus 3, ...) or n constant with k changing. This family covers most Clerk-level series that pass one misses.
4. HARD ABANDON after pass two — see the trick for how to enforce it with a clock rather than by feel.
5. WRONG-NUMBER VARIANT: do not hunt term by term. Apply the pattern forward from term 1 and independently backward from the last term. The single position where the two computations disagree is the wrong term. This is faster than checking each term and it is immune to the trap of assuming term 1 is correct.
6. LETTER SERIES: convert to numbers 1-26 immediately and write the numbers above the letters. Find the pattern in the numbers, compute the answer as a number, then convert back. Do not reason in letters — you cannot subtract letters reliably under a clock.
7. Use EJOTY as the conversion anchor: E is 5, J is 10, O is 15, T is 20, Y is 25. Any letter is then at most two steps from an anchor. Reverse position is 27 minus the forward position (A is 26 from the back, Z is 1).
8. Watch for the two-interleaved-series pattern in letter series: odd-position terms follow one rule and even-position terms another. If a single difference row looks random, split the series into alternate terms before abandoning.
9. ALPHANUMERIC STRING questions: number the elements 1 to n ONCE along the string before reading any question. Then answer positional questions by arithmetic, never by recounting.
10. Collapse compound positional references arithmetically: 'which element is fifth to the left of the twelfth from the left' is simply the seventh from the left, because 12 minus 5 is 7. Similarly 'kth from the right' in an n-element string is position (n + 1 - k) from the left.
11. Verify the answer by substituting it back into the pattern for one step before marking. Two seconds, and it catches the sign errors that cost 0.25 each.

WORKED EXAMPLES (verify them):
A. Missing term: 5, 6, 14, 45, 184, ? First differences are 1, 8, 31, 139 — not clean, so go to pass two. Ratios are roughly 1.2, 2.3, 3.2, 4.1 — near-integer and drifting up, so test times n plus n: 5 times 1 plus 1 is 6; 6 times 2 plus 2 is 14; 14 times 3 plus 3 is 45; 45 times 4 plus 4 is 184. The next step is 184 times 5 plus 5, which is 925. Answer: 925.
B. Wrong term: 2, 3, 8, 27, 110, 565. Forward from term 1 with times n plus n: 2 times 1 plus 1 is 3; 3 times 2 plus 2 is 8; 8 times 3 plus 3 is 27; 27 times 4 plus 4 is 112, not 110. Backward from 565: 565 minus 5 is 560, divided by 5 is 112. Both computations point at position 5, so 110 is the wrong term and should be 112.
C. Letter series: A, C, F, J, O, ? Convert: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. Differences are 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next difference is 6, giving 15 plus 6 which is 21, and 21 is U. Answer: U.
tricks: HARD CAP READ OFF THE ON-SCREEN CLOCK, NOT BY FEEL. The IBPS CBT displays a running sectional countdown. Before you start a series question, note the countdown value. Abandon the question the moment the countdown has fallen by 45 seconds, or the moment pass two ends without a hit — whichever comes first. That is a number you read, not a sensation you judge. In practice at home, use a stopwatch counting up and glance at it once, at the end of pass two. The rule is enforceable precisely because it is tied to two observable events: a clock reading and the completion of pass two.

TWO-PASS PROTOCOL, IN ORDER, NEVER IMPROVISED. Pass one is differences (then second differences). Pass two is ratios and the times-n-plus-k family. Trying patterns in an ad-hoc order is what turns a 25-second question into a 90-second loss, because you revisit the same failed idea twice without noticing. Fixed order also makes the abandon rule meaningful — you always know which pass you are in.

FORWARD-AND-BACKWARD FOR WRONG-NUMBER SERIES. Compute the pattern forward from the first term and backward from the last term. The one position where the two disagree is the wrong term. This halves the checking work and, crucially, it does not assume the first term is correct — which it sometimes is not.

EJOTY PLUS THE 27-RULE. E is 5, J is 10, O is 15, T is 20, Y is 25, and reverse position equals 27 minus forward position. Converting a letter to its number becomes a one-step operation from the nearest anchor instead of counting from A, which is worth roughly 5 seconds per letter and considerably more in a six-term letter series.

NUMBER THE ALPHANUMERIC STRING ONCE, THEN DO ARITHMETIC. Write 1 to n above the elements before reading the questions. Every subsequent positional question — 'fifth to the left of the twelfth from the left' is the seventh from the left; 'eighth from the right' in a 15-element string is the eighth from the left — becomes one subtraction instead of a recount. Across the four or five questions that hang off one string this saves well over a minute.
traps: In a wrong-number series the FIRST term can be the wrong one. Candidates anchor the pattern on term 1 by habit, then reject the correct pattern because it 'fails immediately' — when in fact term 1 is the error.

Stopping the difference analysis after one row. Many Clerk-level series resolve only on second differences, and many letter series resolve only after splitting alternate terms. Abandoning before those two moves throws away questions that were inside the time budget.

'Fifth to the LEFT of the twelfth from the left' is the seventh from the left, not the seventeenth. Candidates add when the direction requires subtraction. Fix the sign by asking which end you are moving toward before computing.
Reverse alphabet position is 27 minus the forward position, not 26 minus. Using 26 shifts every answer by one and is especially damaging in coded-letter series where the shift compounds across terms.

In alphanumeric strings, questions distinguish 'letters', 'digits' and 'symbols' precisely — 'how many digits are immediately preceded by a symbol' is not the same as 'immediately followed by'. Read the preposition; it is the whole question, and both variants appear in the same set.
r-series-num.timeTarget: 25 to 40 seconds per question at mastery, with a hard 45-second abandon read off the clock. A missing-term series that resolves in pass one should take 20 to 25 seconds; one needing pass two, 35 to 45. Wrong-number series run 40 to 55 seconds because of the two-direction check, so budget them slightly higher and abandon at 60. An alphanumeric string with four or five hanging questions should take 20 to 25 seconds to number, then 12 to 18 seconds per question. Across a 5-question series block, the whole block should cost 2:15 to 3:00 out of the 20-minute Reasoning section.
r-series-num.masteryCheck: Forty mixed series questions — 15 missing-term, 10 wrong-number, 15 letter or alphanumeric — attempted with a visible clock: 37 or more correct, average 35 seconds per question, and ZERO questions exceeding the abandon cap. The zero-overrun criterion is the real test; accuracy without timer discipline does not transfer to a 20-minute sectional clock, because the marks a series block costs you are usually spent on the two questions you refused to leave. Log every abandoned question and re-solve it untimed afterwards to check whether your pass-two family needs widening.
questionPatterns: 'What will come in place of the question mark in the following series: 5, 6, 14, 45, 184, ?' — five numeric options.
'Which of the following numbers is wrong in the series 2, 3, 8, 27, 110, 565?' — five options, each a term from the series.
'What will come in place of the question mark: A, C, F, J, O, ?' — five letter options.

'How many such digits are there in the given arrangement, each of which is immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by a letter?' — options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.
'Which element is fifth to the left of the twelfth element from the left end of the given arrangement?' — five options drawn from the string.
'If all the symbols are dropped from the arrangement, which element will be seventh from the right end?' — five options; renumber the shortened string once rather than counting twice.

r-series-num.aiPrompt:
You are setting practice material for IBPS Clerk 2026 Reasoning. Produce a mixed series drill.

PART A — 6 missing-term number series. Each must be solvable by either first or second differences, or by a times-n-plus-k hybrid; do not use patterns requiring third differences or arbitrary primes. Compute each answer yourself and confirm the full pattern holds across EVERY consecutive pair before writing the question.

PART B — 4 wrong-number series of six terms each. In exactly one of the four, make the FIRST term the wrong one, so the solver cannot anchor on it by habit. For each, state the intended pattern and show the forward and backward computations that isolate the wrong term.

PART C — 5 letter or alphanumeric-series questions. Include at least one with two interleaved sub-series (odd positions follow one rule, even positions another) and at least one 15-element alphanumeric string of letters, digits and symbols carrying three positional questions, including one 'kth to the left of the mth from the left' and one 'immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by a letter' with options None / One / Two / Three / More than three.

FORMAT RULES: EVERY question must carry FIVE options labelled (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) — IBPS Clerk papers have five options and never four. Distractors must be plausible near-misses generated by a specific error (off-by-one in the difference row, 26 instead of 27 in the reverse-position rule, adding instead of subtracting in a positional collapse), and for each question name which error produces which distractor.

VERIFY BEFORE OUTPUT: recompute every answer independently and confirm every series resolves exactly. Do not assert correctness in words — print the term-by-term computation for each series alongside the key.

OUTPUT ALSO: for each of the 15 questions, a realistic target time in seconds, and a note on which of the two passes (differences or ratios/hybrids) should have resolved it.
r-series-num.blockPlan: This is a timer-discipline topic, so practise it against a clock from day one — untimed practice actively builds the wrong habit here. DAILY, 20 minutes inside the reasoning hour, split as: 12 minutes on 20 questions with a stopwatch running and the 45-second cap enforced by glancing at the clock at the end of pass two; 5 minutes re-solving untimed only the questions you abandoned, to find out whether your pass-two family is too narrow; 3 minutes updating a running log with two columns — 'resolved in pass one' and 'resolved in pass two'. When the pass-one column stops growing, your difference work is at ceiling and further gains come only from widening the hybrid family. Once a week, run a 10-question block cold inside a full 20-minute sectionally timed reasoning paper, so you rehearse series questions under the same clock as the puzzles. Total commitment is about 2.5 hours a week out of a 28-hour week, which is proportionate to the topic's weight.

Its value is disproportionate to that count for two reasons: each question is independent, so a wrong answer costs one question rather than a whole set of five, and a resolved series takes 25 to 40 seconds against 3 to 4 minutes for a puzzle set. In a 20-minute sectional clock those are the questions that should be banked in the first six minutes. r-coa.whatItIs: Two related 'critical reasoning' formats from the verbal-reasoning family. COURSE OF ACTION (CoA): you get a statement describing a problem or situation, then two (occasionally three) suggested actions numbered I, II, (III). You decide which action(s) logically follow. Five options: (1) Only I follows (2) Only II follows (3) Either I or II follows (4) Neither I nor II follows (5) Both I and II follow. CAUSE & EFFECT: you get two independent statements I and II reporting events, and you classify the relationship. Five options: (1) I is the cause and II is its effect (2) II is the cause and I is its effect (3) Both I and II are independent causes (4) Both I and II are effects of independent causes (5) Both I and II are effects of some common cause. Neither format needs outside knowledge — everything is decided from the words on the page. Both are pure Mains material and are marked at 1.5 marks per question in the 40Q/60-mark Reasoning paper.
r-coa.coreMethod:
COURSE OF ACTION — 5 steps:
1. Read the statement once and underline the HARM WORD — the specific damage, shortage, danger or loss being reported (e.g. 'passengers were injured', 'crop failed', 'accounts were frozen'). Everything is judged against this one word.
2. For each action, apply GATE 1 — RELEVANCE. Does this action act on the harm word or on the mechanism that produced it? If it acts on a different variable, it fails immediately. Do not go further.
3. Apply GATE 2 — FEASIBILITY & AUTHORITY. Can the body named (or clearly implied) actually carry this out with normal powers and normal resources? An action ordering a private citizen or a foreign body to do something fails. Cost alone is NOT a disqualifier unless the statement itself establishes the resource does not exist.
4. Apply GATE 3 — PROPORTIONALITY. Compare the severity of the action to the severity of the harm word. Shutting a whole network because one unit failed is disproportionate; inspecting the whole network is not. Judge against the harm word, never against a feeling that the action 'sounds extreme'.
5. Actions that pass all three gates follow. Evaluate each action INDEPENDENTLY — I following does not make II fail. Choose option (3) 'Either I or II' only when both pass AND they are mutually exclusive (you cannot physically do both) AND each alone fully resolves the harm.

CAUSE & EFFECT — 5 steps:
1. Circle every TIME MARKER before reading for meaning: 'last month', 'recently', 'has decided', 'had been', 'will', 'since Monday'. Chronology decides most of these questions.
2. Order the two events on a timeline. Whichever is EARLIER is the only candidate for cause. An event cannot cause something that already happened.
3. Test the link forward: does the earlier event supply a plausible, direct reason for the later one? If yes, answer (1) or (2) depending on which is earlier.
4. If neither can cause the other, ask: can you NAME a single third event that produced both? Say it out loud in one sentence ('both are government responses to the flood'). If you can name it, answer (5) common cause. If you cannot name it, (5) is wrong.
5. If they are unrelated and each is itself the trigger of something else, answer (3) independent causes. If they are unrelated and each is itself a result of something else, answer (4) effects of independent causes. Ask 'is this statement a trigger or a result?' about each one separately.

WORKED CoA EXAMPLE:
Statement: Several passengers were injured when the floor of a State Transport bus gave way on the highway yesterday.
I. The State Transport Corporation should immediately withdraw all buses of that model from service and inspect their floor and chassis.
II. The State Transport Corporation should stop plying its buses on that highway.
Harm word: passengers injured, caused by structural failure of the bus. Action I acts on the mechanism (bus condition), is within the Corporation's own powers, and is proportionate to injury-causing failure — it FOLLOWS. Action II acts on the highway, which the statement never implicates — it fails Gate 1. Answer: option (1), Only I follows.

WORKED CAUSE & EFFECT EXAMPLE:
I. The State Government has raised the minimum support price of paddy for the current season.
II. Farmers in several districts staged protests last month demanding higher procurement rates.
Time markers: 'current season' (now) vs 'last month' (earlier). II is earlier and supplies a direct reason for I. Answer: option (2), II is the cause and I is its effect.
tricks: Underline the harm word first and answer every CoA option with one question: 'does this touch the harm word?' A CoA that names a different object (the highway, the weather, a different department) is out in about five seconds, before you evaluate whether it is a good idea.

Remember that both actions CAN follow. Roughly one CoA in a set is a pair of complementary actions — one remedial (fix the damage now) and one preventive (stop recurrence). They are not competitors, so both can pass all three gates.
For 'Either I or II', test mutual exclusivity physically: could an administrator sign both files on the same day? If yes, option (3) is impossible and you can eliminate it without reading further.
In cause & effect, do the time-marker scan before you understand the sentences at all. Getting the timeline first removes options (1) or (2) instantly and cuts the question to a two-way choice.

To separate option (3) from option (4), ask of each statement: 'is this something an actor DID, or something that HAPPENED TO people?' Deliberate decisions and policy actions read as causes; price rises, shortages, casualties and closures read as effects.

Do a full 5-question set in one sitting rather than interleaving with puzzles — the format grammar is identical across the set, and staying in one mode saves 5-8 seconds of re-orientation per question.
traps: Rejecting an action just because it is expensive or large-scale. 'The Government should set up a committee to review all bridges in the state' passes Gate 2 — a government can do that. Cost is only a disqualifier when the statement itself says the resource is unavailable.
Choosing option (3) 'Either I or II' whenever both actions look reasonable. Option (3) requires that the two actions cannot coexist. Two reasonable, compatible actions is option (5), Both follow.

Accepting an action that merely restates the problem in imperative form. Statement: 'Road accidents have risen sharply.' Action: 'Road accidents should be reduced.' This names a goal, not an action, and fails Gate 1 — no mechanism is specified.

In cause & effect, marking option (5) common cause simply because the two statements are about the same subject. Two statements can both be about onion prices with one directly causing the other. Same topic is not the same as shared origin.

Reading a future-tense announcement as an effect that has already occurred. 'The company will shut three plants next quarter' has not happened; it cannot be the effect of something reported as happening 'since last week' unless the announcement itself is the event being timed.

Treating a CoA addressed to the general public ('citizens should avoid the area') as automatically invalid. It fails only if no authority could issue it; an advisory issued by the administration named in the statement is a real, executable action.
r-coa.timeTarget: 30-40 seconds per question once the format is drilled. A 5-question set should be finished in 3 minutes flat, which buys you time for the puzzle sets. Never spend more than 60 seconds on one of these — if the timeline is not resolving, mark and move.
r-coa.masteryCheck: Do 10 mixed questions (5 CoA, 5 cause & effect) in 6 minutes and score 8 or more. Additionally, for every action you rejected, be able to state in ONE line which gate it failed (relevance / feasibility / proportionality). If you can pick the right option but cannot name the gate, you are pattern-matching, not reasoning, and the format will break you when the wording shifts.
questionPatterns: Public-safety statement (accident, building collapse, contaminated water) + one action fixing the mechanism and one action fixing an unrelated variable. Five options ending in 'Both I and II follow'.
Administrative statement (a bank's ATM network was down for six hours) + a remedial action and a preventive action, both valid. Correct answer is option (5), Both follow.
Statement with three courses of action I, II and III; options become combinations such as 'Only I and III follow' / 'Only II follows' / 'All three follow' / 'None follows' / 'Only I and II follow'.
Cause & effect with an explicit time gap ('last month' vs 'this week') where the earlier statement plainly explains the later one — tests only chronology.
Cause & effect where both statements are government or corporate announcements made the same week, both traceable to one prior event (a drought, an RBI circular) — tests option (5) common cause.
Cause & effect where the two statements are on the same theme but genuinely unrelated in origin — tests separating option (3) from option (4).

r-coa.aiPrompt:
Act as a question setter for IBPS Clerk Mains 2026 Reasoning Ability. Generate 12 questions: 6 'Statement and Courses of Action' and 6 'Cause and Effect'.

STRICT FORMAT RULES:
- Every question must have EXACTLY FIVE options, labelled (1) to (5). Exactly one is correct.
- For Courses of Action use exactly: (1) Only I follows (2) Only II follows (3) Either I or II follows (4) Neither I nor II follows (5) Both I and II follow.
- For Cause and Effect use exactly: (1) Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect (2) Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect (3) Both statements I and II are independent causes (4) Both statements I and II are effects of independent causes (5) Both statements I and II are effects of some common cause.
- Set the situations in an Indian public-administration or banking context.
- Across the 12 questions, make sure at least one correct answer is option (3), at least one is option (4) and at least one is option (5). Do not let one option dominate.

SOLUTION RULES:
- After all 12 questions, give an answer key and a 2-3 line explanation for each.
- For every Course of Action, state explicitly for EACH action whether it passes or fails on (a) relevance to the harm described, (b) feasibility and authority of the body concerned, (c) proportionality to the harm. Never justify an answer with 'it is generally advisable'.
- For every Cause and Effect, state the chronology of the two events first, then the causal verdict. If you answer (5), NAME the specific common cause in words.
- Do not include any question where two options could both be defended. If you cannot defend exactly one answer, discard and replace the question.
r-coa.blockPlan: One 4-hour day is enough for a first pass; schedule it in the Mains-only phase (after Prelims, i.e. from mid-October 2026). Block 1 (60 min): learn the two option-sets by heart and the three CoA gates; write them on a card. Do 10 CoA questions untimed, writing the failing gate next to each rejected action. Block 2 (60 min): 15 more CoA questions, still writing the gate, but now with a 60-second-per-question cap. Block 3 (60 min): cause & effect from scratch — 15 questions, marking the timeline of both statements before choosing. Block 4 (60 min): 20 mixed questions at 40 seconds each, then review only the wrong ones and classify each error as 'wrong gate' / 'wrong timeline' / 'misread option (3) vs (5)'. Revisit for 30 minutes once a week thereafter; this topic decays fast but relearns fast.

r-coded-dir.whatItIs: A direction-sense question where the relationships are hidden behind symbols instead of being written in words. The paper first gives you a legend — for example 'P $ Q means P is 8 m north of Q', 'P @ Q means P is 6 m east of Q' — and then hands you a chain such as 'A $ B, B @ C, C # D'. You decode the chain into a map and answer the usual direction-sense questions: shortest distance between two points, direction of one point with respect to another, or which points fall in a straight line. Nothing about the geometry is new. The only new thing is a translation layer, and the whole difficulty of the topic lives in translating it without flipping a sign.
r-coded-dir.coreMethod:
1. Read the LEGEND before you read the chain. Copy the symbols into the margin as a small compass cross: north symbol at the top, south at the bottom, east right, west left, with each symbol's distance written next to it. This takes 15 seconds and stops you re-reading the legend six times.
2. Fix the reading convention once, out loud: 'P $ Q means P is north of Q' — the FIRST letter is the one being placed, the SECOND letter is the reference. Write 'first = mover' at the top of your rough work. Every sign error in this topic comes from losing this.
3. Convert to coordinates, not to a drawing. Set North = +y, East = +x. Each coded pair becomes a signed move: 'P $ Q' with $ = 8 m north becomes P = Q + (0, +8). 'P @ Q' with @ = 6 m east becomes P = Q + (+6, 0).
4. Anchor the LAST letter of the chain at (0, 0) and work backwards up the chain. Chains are written so each new letter attaches to the previous one, so walking backwards never forces you to re-anchor and shift every coordinate.
5. Write each letter's coordinate in a vertical list as you go: A (6,8), B (6,0), C (0,0). Do not keep them in your head; the questions will ask about three different pairs.
6. To answer 'direction of X with respect to Y', compute X − Y. Positive x means X is east of Y, positive y means north. If BOTH components are non-zero, the answer is a compound direction (north-east, south-west and so on) — never a plain cardinal one.
7. To answer 'shortest distance', use the straight line: if one component is zero the distance is just the other component; otherwise it is √(Δx² + Δy²). Bank papers pick Pythagorean triples, so recognise 3-4-5, 6-8-10, 5-12-13, 9-12-15, 8-15-17 on sight.
8. If a symbol gives two possible distances ('either 4 m or 9 m'), carry both in a bracket and do not resolve it until a later clue or a question forces one value.

WORKED EXAMPLE (verify every line yourself):
Legend: 'P $ Q' = P is 8 m north of Q; 'P # Q' = P is 8 m south of Q; 'P @ Q' = P is 6 m east of Q; 'P & Q' = P is 6 m west of Q.
Chain: A $ B, B @ C, C # D, D @ E.
Anchor C at (0, 0).
• B @ C → B is 6 m east of C → B = (6, 0).
• A $ B → A is 8 m north of B → A = (6, 8).
• C # D → C is 8 m south of D → C = D + (0, −8), so D = C + (0, +8) = (0, 8). Note this one is read backwards: the coded letter C is the mover, D is the reference, so D sits north of C.
• D @ E → D is 6 m east of E → D = E + (6, 0), so E = D − (6, 0) = (−6, 8).
Final coordinates: A (6, 8), B (6, 0), C (0, 0), D (0, 8), E (−6, 8).
Q: Direction and shortest distance of A with respect to C? A − C = (6, 8). Both non-zero, so A is north-east of C. Distance = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 m.
Q: Direction and distance of E with respect to A? E − A = (−12, 0). Only the x-component is non-zero, so E is due west of A, 12 m away.
tricks: Draw the legend as a compass cross in the margin once, before touching the chain. You will consult it six to eight times across a set; a cross is a glance, a paragraph is a re-read costing about 6 seconds each time.

Use signed coordinates instead of drawing arrows on a map. Adding +6 and −12 is faster and far more reliable than redrawing a figure, and it makes 'which points are in a straight line' a one-glance check (same x, or same y).

Anchor the LAST letter at (0,0) and walk the chain backwards. Chains attach each new letter to the previous one, so backward walking means you never have to translate the whole figure when a later clue lands outside your first sketch.
Memorise the five triples bank papers reuse — 3-4-5, 6-8-10, 5-12-13, 9-12-15, 8-15-17. When Δx and Δy are one of these, the distance is instant instead of a 20-second square-root estimate.

Before computing any square root, check whether one component is zero. If it is, the distance is the other component and there is no root at all. This one glance saves the root on roughly half the questions in a set.
When the legend gives two distances for one symbol, write it as 4/9 in the bracket and keep both branches alive. Committing early forces a full re-solve when the fourth question rules your guess out.
traps: Reading 'A % B' as 'B is south of A'. The coded sentence always describes the FIRST letter's position relative to the second. Getting this backwards mirrors the entire figure, and the mirrored answer is always one of the five options.

Answering 'shortest distance' with the total walked path — adding 6 + 8 = 14 instead of the straight line √(36+64) = 10. The word 'shortest' means straight line between the two named points, never the route length.

Reversing the reference in 'with respect to'. 'Direction of E with respect to A' fixes A as the origin. Swapping them gives the exactly opposite direction, which the paper always includes as a distractor.
Calling a diagonal displacement 'north' because Δy is bigger than Δx. If Δx ≠ 0 and Δy ≠ 0 the answer is compound (north-east, south-west, etc.), regardless of which is larger.

Applying the legend's distance to the wrong symbol when two symbols share a distance value (for example @ and & both 6 m, $ and # both 8 m). The distances match but the axis does not; check the axis, not the number.

Continuing to use coordinates from a previous question's chain when the set gives a fresh chain with the same legend. Re-anchor and rebuild the coordinate list; the legend carries over, the coordinates never do.

questionPatterns: 'What is the shortest distance between point A and point D?' — five distance options in metres, typically including both the straight-line value and the walked-path value as distractors.
'Point E is in which direction with respect to point B?' — five options such as North-East / South-West / South-East / North-West / North.

'If point F is 5 m east of point A, then what is the direction of point F with respect to point D?' — an extra point is injected outside the original chain and must be plotted from an existing coordinate.
'Which of the following sets of points lies in a straight line?' — five triples of letters; the answer is the triple sharing a common x-coordinate or a common y-coordinate.

'What is the total distance covered if a person walks from A to B to C?' — five options; this one asks for path length, not straight-line distance, and sits in the same set as the shortest-distance question to catch you switching.

r-io-1.topicName: Machine input-output I — shifting and arrangement
r-io-1.whatItIs: A 'machine' is given a line of mixed words and numbers (the Input) and rearranges them one step at a time until the arrangement is complete. You are shown a worked Input with its steps, and then given a NEW Input and asked to reproduce specified steps. This first half of the topic covers the two rearrangement families: SHIFTING, where selected elements move to the extreme left or right end and everything else keeps its relative order, and ARRANGEMENT, where the machine sorts words alphabetically and/or numbers in ascending or descending order, building the sorted block from one end. The elements themselves are not altered — only their positions change. There is no cleverness required: the entire topic is 'spot the selection rule, then apply it mechanically'.
r-io-1.coreMethod:
1. Before anything else, compare the INPUT with the LAST GIVEN STEP. Do not start with Step 1. The last step shows you the destination: fully sorted at the left, fully sorted at the right, or sorted at both ends. That single comparison narrows the rule to two candidates in about 20 seconds.
2. Count the elements in the Input. Then count the elements in each step. They must be identical in every step. Write the count at the top of your rough work.
3. Find how MANY elements move per step and from which end. The four standard designs are: one element to the extreme left per step; one to the extreme right per step; one to each end per step (two movers); and a swap of the front and back elements.
4. Find the SELECTION rule — which element is chosen. Test in this fixed order, on Step 1 only: (a) words in dictionary order A→Z, (b) words in reverse dictionary order, (c) numbers ascending, (d) numbers descending, (e) longest/shortest word, (f) largest/smallest number. Stop at the first that fits Step 1.
5. CONFIRM the rule on Step 2 before going further. If Step 2 breaks it, the machine alternates — word one step, number the next — which is the second most common design. Check that before deciding the set is unsolvable.
6. Check what happens to the elements that did NOT move. In a shifting machine they slide one place and keep their relative order among themselves. Verify this once on Step 1; if their relative order changes, it is a full re-sort, not a shift.
7. Write the sorted key sequence in the margin — words alphabetical, numbers ascending — once. Every subsequent step becomes a lookup instead of a fresh sort.
8. The number of steps equals the number of elements that MUST move, which you read straight off the key sequence. Write 'last step = N' before answering anything.
9. Now apply the rule to the new Input. Do not re-derive the rule for each question in the set; it is fixed for all five.

WORKED EXAMPLE (check each line):
Input: 16 gold 52 ring 39 book 74 star   (8 elements)
Step 1: book 16 gold 52 ring 39 74 star
Step 2: book gold 16 52 ring 39 74 star
Step 3: book gold ring 16 52 39 74 star
Step 4: book gold ring star 16 52 39 74
Rule read off: in each step, the word that comes first in the dictionary among the words not yet arranged is pulled out and placed immediately after the already-arranged words at the left end; every other element keeps its relative order and slides right. Words in order: book, gold, ring, star. Four words must move, so there are exactly four steps, and each step still has 8 elements.

APPLY IT to a new Input: 23 lamp 68 cat 41 nest 57 door   (8 elements)
Words alphabetical: cat, door, lamp, nest.
Step 1: cat 23 lamp 68 41 nest 57 door
Step 2: cat door 23 lamp 68 41 nest 57
Step 3: cat door lamp 23 68 41 nest 57
Step 4: cat door lamp nest 23 68 41 57
Last step = Step 4. Check: every step still has 8 elements, and the numbers 23, 68, 41, 57 keep their Input relative order throughout — which is the signature of a shifting machine.
Sample question: which element is third from the RIGHT end in Step 2? Step 2 is cat door 23 lamp 68 41 nest 57. Counting from the right: 57 is first, nest is second, 41 is third. Answer: 41.
tricks: Compare Input against the LAST given step first. Step 1 alone is ambiguous — several rules produce the same first move — but the final step tells you the destination pattern immediately and cuts your rule candidates from six to two.

Count the elements in the Input and write the number at the top. Then count every step you construct. A mismatched count means you have dropped or duplicated an element, and you catch it in 3 seconds instead of discovering it after answering four questions wrongly.
Write the sorted key sequence once in the margin (words A→Z, numbers ascending). Each step then costs one lookup rather than a fresh mental sort of the whole line.

Answer the 'how many steps to complete the arrangement' question FIRST. It needs no intermediate lines — it is just the count of elements that must move — and getting it right confirms your rule before you invest time in step-by-step questions.

Never construct a step you were not asked about, unless a requested step depends on it. In a shifting machine you can often build Step 4 directly from the Input by moving the first four key elements in order.
Write your steps in vertically aligned columns down the page. Position questions ('fourth from the left in Step 3') then become a glance down a column rather than a re-count of the whole line.
traps: Assuming the number of steps equals the number of elements. It equals the number of elements that MOVE. In the worked example the Input has 8 elements but only 4 words move, so the arrangement completes in 4 steps.

Counting the Input as Step 1. The Input is not a step. 'Step 3' means the third line printed after the Input, so an off-by-one here makes every step-specific answer wrong while your rule is perfectly correct.

Applying the word rule on every step when the machine alternates word / number / word / number. If Step 2 does not obey the rule that fit Step 1, test alternation before you conclude the rule is something else entirely.

Assuming dictionary order means A→Z. Some machines sort words in reverse dictionary order and numbers in descending order. Step 1 alone often fits both readings, so check the final step against both before committing.
Counting 'third from the right end' from the left. The paper puts both counts among the five options, so this misread lands cleanly on a wrong option rather than on 'none of these'.

Re-deriving the rule for each of the five questions in the set. The rule is fixed for the whole set; re-deriving costs 40 seconds per question and introduces a fresh chance of reading it differently the second time.
In a shifting machine, re-sorting the unmoved elements. They keep their Input relative order. Sorting them turns a correct rule into a wrong arrangement that still looks plausible.
r-io-1.timeTarget: A full 5-question set in 5–6 minutes: about 60–90 seconds to identify and confirm the rule, then roughly 45 seconds per question. Once fluent, target 4 minutes for the set. If the rule is not confirmed on Step 2 within 2 minutes, leave the set and return only if the section has spare time — with 0.25 negative marking a half-understood machine is five wrong answers, not five right ones.
r-io-1.masteryCheck: On a set you have never seen, you identify and confirm the rule using only Input, Step 1 and Step 2, in under 75 seconds. Then, without writing a single step, you correctly state how many steps the new Input needs. Finally, across five different sets, every step you write has exactly the same element count as its Input — no drops, no duplicates — and you have not once counted the Input as a step.
questionPatterns: 'Which of the following would be Step 3 for the given Input?' — five complete arrangements as options, usually differing only in the position of one or two elements.
'In Step 4 of the given Input, which element is fourth from the left end?' — five options mixing words and numbers.
'How many steps will be required to complete the arrangement?' — five options, typically Four / Five / Six / Seven / None of these.
'In which step is the arrangement "cat door lamp 23 68 41 nest 57" obtained?' — five options including 'There is no such step'.
'Which element is exactly between 68 and 57 in the last step?' — five options; requires you to have built the final step correctly rather than just counted it.

'If in Step 2 all the numbers are interchanged with the words in the same positions, which element would be third from the right end?' — a modification layered on a step you must first construct correctly.
