r-wordpair.topicName: Word pair, number pair, word formation
r-wordpair.whatItIs: The isolated one-liners that fill the gaps between puzzle sets in Prelims. Four sub-types dominate: (1) letter pairs — 'how many pairs of letters in the given word have as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet'; (2) number pairs — the same question asked of the digits in a number against the natural number order; (3) word formation — 'a meaningful word is formed using the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of the word, what is its third letter'; (4) dictionary order and odd-pair-out. These are worth about 2.7 questions in Prelims and 1 in Mains. They are ranked low priority not because the marks are small but because the whole family collapses once alphabet positions are automatic — and there is an exact arithmetic method for letter and number pairs that replaces the scanning most aspirants do.
r-wordpair.coreMethod:
LETTER PAIRS — the two-row method, which is exact, not a shortcut.
The condition 'the two letters have as many letters between them in the word as in the alphabet' says that the gap between their positions in the word equals the gap between their alphabet numbers. Write position index i and alphabet number a for each letter. Then:
- A FORWARD pair (alphabet order matches word order) satisfies a(j) - a(i) = j - i, which rearranges to a - i being EQUAL for both letters.
- A BACKWARD pair (alphabet order reversed) satisfies a(i) - a(j) = j - i, which rearranges to a + i being EQUAL for both letters.
So: 1. Write the word with position numbers 1..n above and alphabet numbers below. 2. Compute the row (a - i) for every letter — every repeated value is one forward pair. 3. Compute the row (a + i) — every repeated value is one backward pair. 4. Read the bracket in the question: 'forward only' means count only the first row; 'both forward and backward' means count both. Two rows of arithmetic replace up to 28 pairwise comparisons.

WORKED EXAMPLE. Word CONTRACT (C O N T R A C T, positions 1 to 8). Alphabet numbers: 3, 15, 14, 20, 18, 1, 3, 20.
Row (a - i): 3-1=2, 15-2=13, 14-3=11, 20-4=16, 18-5=13, 1-6=-5, 3-7=-4, 20-8=12. The value 13 repeats at positions 2 (O) and 5 (R). That is one forward pair: O and R have N, T between them in the word (2 letters) and P, Q between them in the alphabet (2 letters). Correct.
Row (a + i): 3+1=4, 15+2=17, 14+3=17, 20+4=24, 18+5=23, 1+6=7, 3+7=10, 20+8=28. The value 17 repeats at positions 2 (O) and 3 (N). That is one backward pair: O and N are adjacent in the word (0 letters between) and adjacent in the alphabet (0 letters between). Correct.
Answer: 1 forward pair, or 2 pairs counting both directions.

NUMBER PAIRS — identical method with digit values in place of alphabet numbers.
WORKED EXAMPLE. Number 5 8 3 1 9 4 (positions 1 to 6). Row (value - position): 4, 6, 0, -3, 4, -2. The value 4 repeats at positions 1 (digit 5) and 5 (digit 9): 5 and 9 have three digits between them in the number (8, 3, 1) and three between them in counting order (6, 7, 8). One forward pair. Row (value + position): 6, 10, 6, 5, 14, 10. The value 6 repeats at positions 1 (5) and 3 (3): one digit between in the number (8), one between in counting order (4). The value 10 repeats at positions 2 (8) and 6 (4): three digits between in the number (3, 1, 9) and three in counting order (5, 6, 7). Two backward pairs. Total both directions: 3.

WORD FORMATION.
1. Extract the required letters and write them out, keeping them in the order asked. 2. Count the vowels: with none, no English word exists and you mark the 'no such word' option immediately. 3. Build candidates, then answer exactly what is asked — usually a specific letter of the formed word, or 'more than one word', or 'no word'.
WORKED EXAMPLE. 'If a meaningful four-letter word is formed using the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of CHARTER, what is the third letter of that word?' CHARTER is C(1) H(2) A(3) R(4) T(5) E(6) R(7). The extracted letters are C, A, T, R. The only common English word is CART. Its third letter is R.

DICTIONARY ORDER. Compare first letters only; descend to the second letter only on a tie, and so on. A shorter word that is a prefix of a longer one comes first (CAR before CARD).
tricks: The two-row method. Computing (alphabet number minus position) and (alphabet number plus position) turns an eight-letter word into two rows of eight numbers and a duplicate hunt — about 25 seconds — instead of up to 28 pairwise comparisons that take well over a minute and miss pairs.
Read the bracket before computing. 'In the forward direction only' means you compute one row, not two, halving the work. Most aspirants compute both and then discard half.

Count the vowels first in word-formation questions. Zero vowels means no meaningful word exists and the answer is the 'no such word can be formed' option in about five seconds, with no letter-shuffling at all.
In dictionary-order questions, compare only first letters on the first pass. Five-option sets usually separate on letter one, and descending to letter two is needed for at most one tie.

Never alphabetise the word before scanning for pairs. The condition is defined on the positions in the word as written; reordering it silently changes every position index and produces a wrong count that still looks tidy.
traps: Counting 'letters between them' inclusively. A and B have zero letters between them, not one. Every option list contains the answer produced by the inclusive reading.

Counting positions from the wrong end. When the question says 'the 3rd, 5th and 7th letters from the right end', counting from the left extracts a different letter set that still forms a plausible word, and that word is one of the five options.
Skipping repeated letters. If a word contains two Ts, they occupy two distinct positions and each must appear separately in both rows — dropping the duplicate loses a real pair.

Accepting proper nouns, abbreviations or foreign words in word formation. Only common English words count, and letter sets that only form a proper noun are constructed to make you answer 'yes' when the correct option is 'no such word'.
Treating a shorter word as later in dictionary order. CAR comes before CARD; the prefix always precedes the longer word.
Applying the two-row method to the alphabetised version of the word rather than the word as printed, which is the single most common way the method is misused.
r-wordpair.timeTarget: Letter-pair question with the two-row method on a seven or eight letter word: 30-40 seconds. Number-pair question on a six or seven digit number: 25-35 seconds. Word formation: 25-35 seconds, or under 10 seconds when the vowel count is zero. Dictionary order: 15-20 seconds. Since these arrive as standalone one-liners, target three of them inside 100 seconds of the Prelims clock.
r-wordpair.masteryCheck: Thirty mixed questions (letter pair, number pair, word formation, dictionary order) in 15 minutes with at least 28 correct. Every letter-pair and number-pair item must be solved by writing the two rows on the rough sheet — if you scanned instead, the item does not count even when correct. Separately, produce the two rows for a nine-letter word in under 30 seconds.
questionPatterns: Letter pair, one direction. 'How many pairs of letters are there in the word CONTRACT, each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet, in the forward direction only?' Five options: One, Two, Three, More than three, None.
Letter pair, both directions. The same question on a different word with '(both forward and backward)' in the bracket. Five options.
Number pair. 'How many pairs of digits are there in the number 583194, each of which has as many digits between them in the number as when the digits are counted in ascending order?' Five options.

Word formation. 'If a meaningful four-letter word is formed using the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of the word CHARTER, what is the third letter of that word? If no such word can be formed mark X, and if more than one such word can be formed mark Y.' Five options.
Dictionary order. 'If the words BANKER, BANNER, BANGLE, BASKET and BATTLE are arranged as in a dictionary, which word comes third?' Five options, one per word.

r-wordpair.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk 2026 reasoning trainer. Generate 24 miscellaneous alphabet-and-word questions. HARD FORMAT RULE: every question must have exactly FIVE options labelled (a) to (e). Never four. Composition: 8 letter-pair questions on seven-to-nine letter words (4 specifying forward direction only, 4 specifying both forward and backward, and at least 2 using words containing a repeated letter), 5 number-pair questions on six- or seven-digit numbers, 6 word-formation questions (2 where exactly one word is formable, 2 where more than one is formable, 1 where no word is formable because no vowel is extracted, 1 counting letters from the right end), and 5 dictionary-order questions including one pair where a shorter word is a prefix of a longer one. For every letter-pair and number-pair question, before printing it, compute both the (value minus position) row and the (value plus position) row yourself, list every duplicate you found and the actual pair it corresponds to, and confirm the stated answer matches. For word-formation questions, list every English word the letter set can form and confirm the count. Then give an answer key with those rows and word lists shown. Do not include any advice about which option is statistically likely.
r-wordpair.blockPlan: 60-minute Reasoning block. 0-15 min concept: derive the two-row method yourself — write the condition a(j) - a(i) = j - i and rearrange it to a - i = a - i, then do the same for the backward case. Work the CONTRACT and 583194 examples in coreMethod by hand and check your rows against the ones given. 15-35 min untimed: 20 questions across all four sub-types, no clock, writing both rows for every pair question. 35-55 min timed: 25 fresh questions in 12 minutes, then 8 minutes of review; for every missed pair, find which row would have caught it. 55-60 min error log: classify errors as inclusive-counting, wrong end, repeated letter dropped, proper noun accepted, or method applied to the alphabetised word.

r-coded-blood.whatItIs: A Mains topic in which family relationships are hidden behind symbols. A legend defines a small set of symbols — for example 'A + B means A is the father of B', 'A - B means A is the sister of B', 'A x B means A is the mother of B', 'A / B means A is the brother of B' — and you are given an expression such as 'P x Q / R + S' and asked how P is related to S. The second question shape reverses it: 'Which of the following expressions shows that M is the mother of T?', with five candidate expressions to test. It carries zero weight in Prelims and about 2.7 questions in Mains, where each question is worth 1.5 marks. The difficulty is not the family logic — that is the same tree you already draw for direct blood relations — it is the legend direction and the strict adjacency rule, both of which are read wrong under a 35-minute clock.
r-coded-blood.coreMethod:
1. Rewrite the legend before touching the expression. For every symbol, record three things in a compact key: the gender of the LEFT person (M, F or ?), the generation arrow (up-arrow means the left person is one level above the right, right-arrow means same level, down-arrow means one level below), and whether it is a blood link or a marriage link. Four symbols become four two-character notes and the rewriting takes about 15 seconds.
2. Read the expression strictly left to right, and apply each symbol ONLY to the two letters immediately adjacent to it. In 'P x Q / R', the slash connects Q and R. It never connects P and R.
3. Draw as you go, using the standard tree: spouses on one horizontal line joined by a double line, siblings on one horizontal line joined by a single line, children one level below on a vertical line. Write the level number (0, -1, -2) beside each letter as you place it, so the final gap is read off rather than recomputed.
4. Name the answer from the drawn tree using level gap plus gender plus side: gap 2 and female is grandmother, gap 1 and male is father, gap 0 with shared parents and male is brother, gap 0 across a double line is husband or wife.
5. For 'which expression shows...' questions, first eliminate options by the required GENDER. If the target relation needs a female and an option's symbol chain never forces that person female, discard it without drawing. Then draw only the surviving options.
6. Never invent unstated family members. If a symbol only says 'sibling' or 'child', the gender stays a question mark, and 'cannot be determined' is a legitimate derived answer.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1. Legend: 'A + B' means A is the father of B; 'A - B' means A is the sister of B; 'A x B' means A is the mother of B; 'A / B' means A is the brother of B. Expression: 'P x Q / R + S'. How is P related to S?
P x Q: P is the mother of Q, so P is female at level 0 and Q sits at level 1. Q / R: Q is the brother of R, so Q is male and R sits at level 1 as Q's sibling. R + S: R is the father of S, so R is male and S sits at level 2. Because P is Q's mother and R is Q's sibling, P is also R's mother. The path from P to S runs P, then her child R, then R's child S. Level gap 2, P is female, so P is the grandmother of S (specifically the paternal grandmother, since the link runs through S's father).

WORKED EXAMPLE 2. Same legend. Expression: 'M / N x O - T'. How is M related to T?
M / N: M is the brother of N, so M is male, level 0, N at level 0. N x O: N is the mother of O, so N is female and O sits at level 1. O - T: O is the sister of T, so O is female and T sits at level 1 as O's sibling. Since N is O's mother and T is O's sibling, N is also T's mother. M is N's brother, and N is T's mother, so M is T's mother's brother: M is the maternal uncle of T.

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 (reverse shape, why gender elimination works). Same legend. Suppose the question asks which expression shows that D is the daughter of B. The relation requires D to be female and one level below B. A candidate expression in which D only ever appears to the left of the slash (brother) fixes D as male and is eliminated without drawing anything at all. Only expressions that force D female through the minus symbol (sister) plus a parental link, or through a symbol explicitly defining 'daughter of', survive to the drawing stage.
tricks: Rewrite the legend as a gender-plus-arrow key before reading the expression. Four two-character notes cost 15 seconds and remove the single largest error source in the topic, which is re-reading the legend halfway through and reversing it.

Write the level number beside each letter as you place it. When the third question on the same expression asks a different relation, you read the gap off the sheet in about three seconds instead of re-walking the tree.
Draw the tree once per expression. Mains sets typically hang two or three questions on one expression, so the 40-second build amortises to roughly 15 seconds per question.
Gender-eliminate before drawing in 'which expression shows...' questions. Discarding two or three of the five options on gender alone converts a 90-second question into a 55-second one.

Finish by chaining to a familiar word: gap 2 plus female equals grandmother, gap 1 plus male equals father, gap 0 plus shared parents plus male equals brother. Naming from the gap avoids the retracing that produces mirror-relation errors.
traps: Reversing the legend. 'A + B means A is the father of B' does not mean B is the father of A. Some question sets deliberately phrase one symbol as 'A + B means B is the father of A' to punish skim-reading. Underline whose role is stated first, every time.
Applying a symbol to non-adjacent letters. In 'P x Q / R', the slash relates Q and R only. Linking P and R produces a tree that is internally consistent and completely wrong.

Assigning a gender to a gender-neutral code. 'A is the child of B', 'A is the sibling of B' and 'A is the spouse of B' fix nothing. An answer built on a guessed gender is wrong even when the structure is right, and 'cannot be determined' will be among the five options.
Checking only the structure in 'which of the following is true' questions. 'Q is the nephew of P' fails if Q is female even when the structural link is exactly right.
Losing the level count across four symbols. Recomputing the gap at the end, rather than reading the level numbers you wrote as you drew, is where the answer flips between grandmother and mother.
Answering the mirror relation. 'How is P related to S' asks for P's role. If P is S's grandmother, the answer is grandmother, and 'granddaughter' is one of the five options.

Inventing family members to make a count work. For 'how many female members are there in the family' questions, count only people the expression actually names and only genders the symbols actually force.
r-coded-blood.timeTarget: Legend rewrite plus tree for a four-letter expression: 40-50 seconds. Each additional question on the same tree: 10-15 seconds. A three-question Mains set on one expression: 80-100 seconds. Single 'which expression shows...' questions: 50-70 seconds, because up to five expressions must be evaluated — gender elimination is what keeps this under 70.
r-coded-blood.masteryCheck: Twenty coded blood relation questions in 15 minutes with at least 18 correct, including at least five 'which expression shows...' items in which you recorded a reason for rejecting each of the four wrong options. Every legend must have been rewritten as a gender-plus-arrow key before solving, and every letter in every expression must carry a level number on your rough sheet.
questionPatterns: Single expression, single question. Legend of four symbols, then 'P x Q / R + S. How is P related to S?' Five options including grandmother, grandfather, mother, aunt and cannot be determined.
Single expression, three questions. One six-letter expression with three questions hung on it: one relation, one 'how many female members', one 'which pair is a couple'. Each with five options.
Reverse shape. 'Which of the following expressions shows that D is the daughter of B?' Five candidate expressions as options, at least two of which are structurally right but fix the wrong gender.
Gender-neutral legend. A legend in which one symbol means 'A is the child of B' or 'A is the sibling of B', with a question whose correct answer is 'cannot be determined' out of five options.

Reversed-direction legend. A legend containing one symbol phrased as 'A @ B means B is the husband of A', with a relation question that only resolves correctly if that reversal was noticed. Five options.
